SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
INTERVIEWS WITH JAZZ MUSICIANS
MARY LOU WILLIAMS
Jazz Oral History Project
Interviewed by John S. Wilson
on 6/26/1973
Let's start from the beginning. When were you born and where?
I was born in Atlanta, Georgia, 1910, 8th of May.
8th of May, 1910. What was your name when you were born?
Mary Louise Scruggs. That was my father's name. I was born out of wedlock.
Did you know your father?

I met my father. Before I went to Europe I had to go to Atlanta, Georgia, to find out my birth date, because it seems that during the period when I was born they had these - what do they call the women that delivered babies?
Midwives.
Midwives, and my mother didn't really remember my birth date. I couldn't get it in Pittsburgh so I had to go back to Atlanta, Georgia, to try to get it.
And you met your father there?
No. I met him in 1952.
How did you run into him then?
I have a half-brother in Atlanta, Georgia. He's a school teacher -
What's his name?
Willis Scruggs. He was just a little boy when I was about 2 or 3 years old. He just loved music arou
WILLIAMS

the house and he played and he's always had an admiration for my playing, to note that I had started so early. When I went to Atlanta, Georgia to try to get a birth certificate he took me out to meet my Dad.
You met him?
Yes, I met him.
How did you get along?

Well, the one thing that was a drag to me, he says, "You know who I am?" I said, "No." He said, "I'm your father. What'd you bring me?" I said, "Of all things, you've never done anything for me." So that ruined my day almost.
That was the end of your father as far as you were concerned. Did you know anything about his background at all?

No. I'm from a family that never talked much about backgrounds and what-not, except for a few things that I learned from them at an early age. I used to, as a young kid, I'd sneak under the bed and listen to their conversation and I learned a great deal about the past through that. They never allowed the kids to sit in on conversations when they had company or anything like that.
But this was not in relation to your father?
No, I never knew about him at all. I never knew that I was born out of wedlock until I was 10 or 12 years
WILLIAMS
old and a relative of mine got angry with me and said, 'You grew up like a weed. You don't even belong to the family,' or something like that. Then I discovered it.
How did you feel?
I felt very discouraged but I've always been a strong person. I've never allowed anything to linger long with me to make me feel unhappy. I'd turn it off and go out and play or do something.
Now your mother. What was her name?

Virginia Burley, B-u-r-l-e-y. She was born in Atlanta, Georgia, and she played piano for the church, danced for the church to raise money. She said that they'd pull a curtain down across the pulpit and she'd dance to raise money for the church and she also played for the church. When I was around between 2 and 3 she said I was always getting into things as a child, was a nervous baby. She was nervous all the time she was practicing the organ so she decided to put me on her lap while she was practicing. She said one day while she had me on her lap I started picking out melodies. It must have been unusual because she dropped me and ran out to call the neighbors to come in and hear it. From that day on she had professional musicians around me like Jack Howard. He was a terrific boogie-woogie pianist you see, who played rag-time. This was in Atlanta, Georgia. I was still there. I didn't leave Atlanta until I was
WILLIAMS

around 4, 5, or 6. You lose track of the dates and age but I know that I was at least 4 or 5. So she had Jack Howard and professional musicians to come in. I like Jack Howard because he played such a strong piano he could break up all the pianos and as a baby I started playing like that. I think I got the masculine quality from him, of playing.
At that early age did you have any professional teachers?

No, my mother wouldn't allow anyone to teach me because she took one lesson and after that she couldn't improvise any more. So she allowed no one to teach me and I'm very happy that she didn't because later on I discovered that I had a strong pitch, perfect pitch. In Pittsburgh I found out. I happened to be sitting in a class and the teacher had lost her harp. She couldn't give the class the tone to start their singing, so I told her I could do that, and she was surprised when I did it. She went out in the hall where the piano was and I had given her the right tone, and I discovered that I had perfect pitch.
Are there dangers in having perfect pitch or is it just a help?

It's a great help. It's a danger in studying early because you may lose it. I know some, great musicians that never lost it, like Dizzy Gillespie, but it's a danger in losing it through studying music, you know.
Why does studying make you lose it?
WILLIAMS

Well, because everything's on paper and you don't get any more sounds or anything. I think it's best, especially in jazz, for a musician to learn to feel everything and teach himself. If he's going to play the classics - like one summer I went to a teacher for about 2 weeks and I knew what to do, you see, but there's a danger in losing the feeling in jazz because it's a self-taught music and since I was going to play nothing but jazz I benefited by not studying...
How did you know you were going to play nothing but jazz?

Well, I never really knew but my guidance in life - I never really knew what I was going to do. I think God was working me towards doing greater things - I have a feeling about God using certain people to help others and they're - they really don't know what they're going to do but it works out that they're doing a terrific job for Him, and that has been my whole life. I never knew that I was going to play jazz or the classics but I knew that I loved jazz.
We'll get to that as we get along. But getting back to Atlanta, did you have any brothers or sisters then?
Oh, many, maybe nine or eleven. Twins - I have two twins that were born on the same day I was born but a different year, the 8th of May.

SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
INTERVIEWS WITH JAZZ MUSICIANS
MARY LOU WILLIAMS
Jazz Oral History Project
Interviewed by John S. Wilson
on 6/26/1973
Let's start from the beginning. When were you born and where?
I was born in Atlanta, Georgia, 1910, 8th of May.
8th of May, 1910. What was your name when you were born?
Mary Louise Scruggs. That was my father's name. I was born out of wedlock.
Did you know your father?

I met my father. Before I went to Europe I had to go to Atlanta, Georgia, to find out my birth date, because it seems that during the period when I was born they had these - what do they call the women that delivered babies?
Midwives.
Midwives, and my mother didn't really remember my birth date. I couldn't get it in Pittsburgh so I had to go back to Atlanta, Georgia, to try to get it.
And you met your father there?
No. I met him in 1952.
How did you run into him then?
I have a half-brother in Atlanta, Georgia. He's a school teacher -
What's his name?
Willis Scruggs. He was just a little boy when I was about 2 or 3 years old. He just loved music arou
WILLIAMS
It was because I had taken the neighborhood on.
This was after, um in Pittsburgh, in East Liberty.
Yes.
Down in Atlanta, you stayed there until what - 3 or 4?
Until I was, I think, 3 or 4. It's difficult, it's been so long, to remember how old I was because I never heard them tell me how old I was when we left Atlanta. I think I was between 3 and 4.
Do you know how old your mother was when you left Atlanta?
No. I know one time in Pittsburgh we had one of the youngest generations in America, it was listed as that in Pittsburgh.
You and your mother?
See, my great-grandmother was living when I was born and my sister got married before she died and had a little baby. I think my mother must have married when she was 16.
You mentioned your great-grandmother. This was on your mother's side?
My mother's side.
Did they all come from Atlanta?
They all came from Atlanta.
And had been there for several generations?
WILLIAMS 8
Yes, Atlanta.
Aside from your mother, were they musical particularly?
No, I think only my mother and myself. My brother, the twin brother - you know, the two twins I mentioned - he was musical but he didn't work at it. He could dance and play a little piano.
When you started picking out those tunes on your mother's lap, do you know now what you were doing?
No, that's the strange thing, I didn't know what I was doing.
I mean do you know the tunes now? Did your mother tell you?

No, when I played the History of Jazz I played the same tune that she taught me... it was a rag-time. we called it 'Fandango' And "Mother Pin a Rose on Me", my stepfather taught me that when I was - I used to play that.
This was, when you talk of your stepfather, Fletcher Burley?
Fletcher Burley.
So that gets us up into Pittsburgh. Why did your mother leave Atlanta?
Well, I don't know. I think they just moved away because they had a yearning to go. My grandmother's sister, all her sisters, had moved I guess years previously
WILLIAMS

and so they decided to go and move to Philadelphia, also her mother, my grandmother Mrs.(Rouser)- Anna Jane(Rouser) rather - and her mother was also there, the Parkers, and her father, in Pittsburgh, so I think they decided to go there to be with the family.
So you're maybe roughly 4 years old when you get to Pittsburgh?
Yes.
What was the family life like then? Your mother was not married at this point?
No, I think she married Fletcher Burley about a year later.
And she was living with her sister?
She was living with her aunt, my grandmother's sister.
I see. When she married Fletcher Burley did she still live there or did you all move somewhere else?

We lived there for a while. I started to school there and then we moved to Euclid Avenue in East Liberty; later on Wilmington Avenue and Hamilton Avenue after that. We moved about 3 different places before the family really became settled.
Once you got to Pittsburgh do you remember early years of playing piano?
I never stopped playing piano. I had a cousin
WILLIAMS

that used to dance and we'd make a little money dancing. At one time when I was about 6 or 7 years old I made more money than my stepfather by this. The teachers used to take me home with them and give me a little handkerchief pocket full of money. I'd play for the (musician?), they'd give a little afternoon tea. I'd have to sit on someone's lap, I was so small. I'd play for the little teas and for the neighborhood. I'd charge a dollar an hour.
What did you play mostly?

All requests. I couldn't read piano and - well, this is getting a little ahead of it, but I'll talk about it now while it's on my mind. When I was 10 or 12 I played with a union band there and tunes like "The Doll Dance" I couldn't read it but I had such a terrific ear that after they played the first chorus, I knew it. They'd have the music up in front of me and I never even told them I couldn't read it. But it must have been all right and no complaints because I was hired from year to year to play with them.
Were you a member of the union?

No. The strangest thing happened after the musicians found out that I was playing with them. They used to come by the house, when I was between the ages of 8 and 10 or 12, when I was in grade school, and take me out. and pick me up mother, a I had a family that didn't mind. In the beginning they had an older member to go with me and after a while some
WILLIANS
musician would get her confid_ence, gain her confidence and then she'd allow me to go with them.
At this stage were you just playing what people wanted you to play or were there certain kinds of things that you liked to play?

Well, I played anything they asked me to play. There were certain things that I played, like Fats Waller - I'd get his records. My stepfather bought me a piano but it was a what-do-you-call-it - set player? - style where you had rolls - player piano. I learned the classics from that.
How? By watching the keys?

The keys, my fingers would go down on the keys, yes... I had 3 people in the family - my grandfather, my uncle, and my stepfather, that would give me a weekly allowance to play their favorite tunes. My uncle liked Irish songs. My grandfather liked the classics and my stepfather liked boogie-woogie, so he'd give me more money than my - my uncle or grandfather would give me 50¢ a week and he'd give me 15 or 20.
You mean, if the one that liked classics had given you $25 -
50¢ a week.
A little more you might have ended up playing classical music?
WILLIAMS
I don't think so because I liked jazz.
When did you start playing with any regularity anywhere? Was it during this period?

From the age of 6 until I was 14 I was all over the city playing. I played for the Mellons. I became the little piano girl of East Liberty and anytime anybody was having a party or anything they'd say, "Well, let's get the little piano girl." So by this time I was among nothing but the wealthy people of Pittsburgh, playing for their parties. The chauffeur would pick me up or my stepfather, Fletcher Burley, would take me. He would take me to parties like for the Mellons and my brother-in-law, Hugh Floyd, would take me to theatres to keep my ears open and listen to musicians. Sometimes I would go to sleep and he'd throw me over his shoulder and bring me home.
So you were getting real training?
Yes. Roland Mayfield later on - there were 3 important people in my life, including the pianist that I spoke about -
Jack Howard.
Jack Howard. There was Roland Mayfield, when I was stranded at the age of 12 - I'd go out by myself a lot and he'd get in his car and pick me up and bring me home.
Who was Roland Mayfield?
Roland Mayfield was a very important man.
WILLIAMS

He was what you call a sportsman; he had a nightclub and he became very wealthy among the people there in East Liberty and he was called the Black Prince of East Liberty. I met him when I was 12 years old. He taught me to drive a car. In fact there was about 6 young girls where we went to school. They could all drive but they had to ask me if they could drive the car. He played a very important part in my career.
In what ways?

He would always pick me up or give me anything that I needed. I would never write home and ask anybody for anything when I was out on the road. He would ask, "How's the kid?... She don't look and sound too good." He'd jump in his car, I don't care what was happening, even at work in his place of business, and pick me up and bring me home.
How about Jack Howard?

Jack Howard was an influence as far as giving me strength on the piano. He told me always to play the left hand louder than the right because that's where the beat and the feeling was. It's just like a drum keeping a steady beat. He taught me a lot of professional things it would have taken me years and years to learn.
You first met him in Atlanta?
Yes. The first date that I began to play my mother got him to come in...
And then he was in Pittsburgh later?
Yes, he came to Pittsburgh. In fact all my mother's
WILLIAMS
friends came to Pittsburgh.
Who was the third influence?
Fletcher Burley, my stepfather.
What sort of a man was he?

He was the kind of a man that he loved me so much he would almost put his own kids aside for me, if I needed anything. Well, he was very charitable. Sometimes I'd bring kids in that didn't have shoes and he'd give them money to buy shoes or to buy clothing. Fletcher had a big coat - this is funny - he had a big oversized coat made and he took me in gambling joints and everywhere and he'd put me under this coat because.... (NOT CLEAR) He was considered a very good, bad man, not overbearing but he was treacherous if you made him angry. Everybody in Pittsburgh knew about this and nobody even tried to harm me. But he was a very sweet man. He'd say, "Stop the game. I want you to hear my little girl play." He'd put a dollar in the hat and then they'd pass the hat around after I had finished and he'd take me outside and he'd say, "Give me my dollar back."... My mother didn't know what he was doing until three years ago. I was talking to her and she said 'My Goodness, you didn't tell me!'
Who else was an influence?
Just a few. They were big influences people of course in music.
Was Fletcher Burley....?
Yes, he was, but he was a strange man. He would
WILLIAMS

not gamble. He worked every day; he would not gamble with that money. He'd take the money home and give it to my mother for her bills and what-not and he'd go up the street and have a friend throw him in the game. That's what they called it - that is, give him a stake in the game. He was a terrific gambler.
Now you talked about Roland Mayfield coming out and getting you when you were stranded. Were you touring the whole time -

I was with home talent shows and things like that. I was talking to him one time, "Roland, do you remember when you picked me up in New York when I was stranded?" He said, "New York, Buffalo, Cincinnati, Chicago, Cleveland, Steubenville."
When did you start playing at something more than parties?
Do you remember the Cotton Pickers?
McKinney's Cotton Pickers?

Yes. When I was in around 5th or 6th grade they used to come to Pittsburgh and they'd drive this big bus on our street, all these musicians, Chu Berry and all of them would take me out on gigs with them.
Because you were that well known?
Yes. I was well known by musicians. When they'd come to Pittsburgh they'd come by and pick me up and take me out with them. I went out with the home
WILLIAMS

talent show then. The first time I left really professionally is when a show came to Pittsburgh and the pianist, something happened to him so the Western Union boy hdd delivered a wire to the owner of the show. The owner told him, "My goodness, I need a pianist. I've got to go out..." He said, "I know who you should get, the little piano girl." He said, "What?" He said, "Come and go with me, I'll take you to East Liberty to her house." So he brought this man all the way - about 8 miles from downtown to East Liberty. When the manager drove up I was on the sidewalk playing Hop Scotch with the kids. He was so angry and upset because he didn't have much time before the show that night. He said, "Why would you take up so much of my time bringing me out here?" He said, "Wait till you hear her play." So he went in and out, and he asked me if I could memorize and I said yes. He hummed the entire show to me and I memorized it. That night I played it.
Was any of it material you had heard before?

Nothing I had heard before - Bandanna Days and all that kind of thing, I had never heard them before. You know during that period they were all tunes like that, like old-fashioned, like, I don't know what you'd call them, but they were like minstrel show tunes, you know? So I went up - he had to go to a notary with my mother so that I'd be able to go out. It was during the summer vacation
WILLIAMS
and school was out, so my mother signed papers for me to go out with a lady. I worked with him about two months until school opened in September.
Whereabouts did you go?
I went to all these little cities like Springfield, Ohio, Springfield something, Indianapolis -
One-nighters?
No, weekly shows.
What kind of a show was this?
Vaudeville, the worst...T.O.B.A, you've heard of that. Tough On Black Actors.
Was this Brodson Harris? 'Buzzin'
Brodson Harris. Buzzin'
What did he do?
He was the owner of the show.
He didn't perform?
Yes, he was a comedian, a very good one, a black-face comedian.
So when you got back from your summer's tour, what became of your career then?
Well I was still in school, in school for a long time, but see I'd go out in summer vacations. One time I ran away and my mother came and got me.
Where did you go? Why did you run away?
Well, because I had that blood in me like a gypsy. I wanted to go out and play, be with musicians.
WILLIAMS
How old were you?

I really don't know. I was under 16 because you know, because when I played with Duke Ellington's Washingtonians I was between 16 and 17. I just found a date I went to Pittsburgh... I have some stockings, my first stockings that I wore with Seymour and Jeanette; I'll show them to you later. I just washed them last night. Peter brought all these things out in a trunk and so I found the date. It was in about '25 or '26 when I was with Seymour and Jeanette.
You mean you washed them and they didn't fall apart?
No. I'll show them to you; they're wonderful. I have all the first things that I wore with them, except the shoes and the dress. You were asking me about -
About your touring after that summer with Buzzin' Fredeson Harris. The home talent show - you were going to tell me about the home talent show.
Well, in Washington, Pennsylvania - I went there and she didn't know where I was so she found out where I was through a friend.
Was this your mother?
Yes, my mother, so she came there and picked me up. I was kind of glad because the owner of the show - they had these young kids, 12 and 14, 15 years old, and this
WILLIAMS

man was not too good. One person I appreciate very much and she was a very good friend, she was 18. She watched over these kids. This man had taken 3 of us into a room and I never had a drink in my life except once when I was a little baby.
How did you get in contact with this man?

He knew about me. By this time everybody knew about me, even musicians from New York. I was playing a style of piano that must have been amazing to them but it was nothing to me. You know, I never had a needle or anything, I was just playing, that's all, but it reached musicians in New York and everywhere knew about my playing.
Well, did the man come to your house?
For the home talent, yes. They usually called - we didn't have a phone then - they got in touch. It seemed that everybody knew about me all over East Liberty and downtown.
Do you remember this man's name?
No, I don't remember his name and happy I forgot it, because he was not too nice with these kids.
He got you and the other girls in a room?
In a room and he was giving us whiskey and Coca-Cola, and Margaret came in. He was just about to do his act, you know, and she came into the room. I was so sick.
WILLIAMS

He put it in Cola-Cola and we thought we were drinking Coca-Cola. None of us knew the taste of whiskey. She came in and she took a stick and she was beating all over his head. Margaret Warren, she was beautiful. She was watching over us and we didn't even know it.
What became of the home talent show?
He was the one that got this home talent, the manager of the home talent.
Was this the beginning of it or the break-up of it?

No, the beginning of it was, we rehearsed and we did the home talent show in Pittsburgh. Then we ventured out to Washington, Pennsylvania, to a theatre there, to do the same show and he had all these young kids with him.
So was that as far as you got, just to Washington?
Yes. Margaret pulled out and took 3 of us home with her.
Did you work with her again?
Yes, with the Buzzin' Harris show, and I always had that same protection from her.
So this is another person that -?
Yes, Margaret Warren. She was such a beautiful person. She would walk over and you wouldn't even know it. She was so quiet and easy going, just a beautiful person.
What became of her, do you know?
WILLIAMS
She's still in Pittsburgh; I just saw her when I did the Mass there. She was dancing with the chorus, you see. She was teaching the girls. She was 18 herself but we were 14, 15 years old.
Earlier you mentioned about your listening to Fats Waller records. What else were you listening to?

Jelly Roll Morton and Willie the Lion. I didn't get many of his records. I had copies of Jelly Roll's records. I happened to go to New York one time and I was playing his 'Pearls' and he, you know how he was, a little irritable and he said, "You don't play it like that! You play it like this!" And then he showed me how he wanted me to play it.
But back in an earlier stage in Pittsburgh you were listening to Waller and to Jelly Roll and to Willie the Lion?
Jelly Johnson's rolls for the set player.
After the home talent show what happened next?
John Williams - I later married him, you know, my first husband - joined up with the Harris Buzzin' Harris show in Cleveland.
You went out twice with that show?
I went out twice. The second time John Williams and his combo joined it.
But the first time was just summer vacation?
Yes.
WILLIAMS
And then in about a year or so, was this a summer vacation?

I really don't know whether it was summer vacation but I decided to go out and stay out, which I didn't. I had to come back and go to school again. I went to Cleveland and several other places and by that time John Williams had joined with a small combo and he won my mother's confidence. He was very smart. He really should have been a psychiatrist because the things he did to help Andy Kirk in the band, keeping him down dissenting and all that and making a guy play and do his instrument was really terrific.
How old was he when you first met him?
He must have been around 19 or 20. I think he's about 5 or 6 years older than I am, something like that.
You were 14?

Yes, I was... He had a small combo, it was the most terrific thing you've ever heard in your life. See, John was the first musician that ever played a baritone and he was really in demand all over the country, everybody heard about him. But he chose to work with other people, you know, and he had his own little combo. We had a trombone player there that played more trombone with his foot than I hear today.
What was his name?
Sylvester Briscoe. His music was just terrific.
WILLIAMS
Buzzin
When you went out with the Harris show were you just part of the band or did you have a special spot of your own?

No, no special, all I did was I played for the show and when they were short a chorus girl I'd go up on the stage and dance. I never did a solo but we did a combo. You know that was during the era in the 20's of the jazz band, you know, small combos and all they did was clown. A lot of music was coming out of the horns but there was a lot of clowning. That was the jazz band era...
What sort of clowning?
Oh, I'd play music and I'd turn around on the stool... I used to put a sheet over the keys and play with my elbows...
How did you do that?

Just did it. You know I used to sit at the piano, my brother-in-law said, when I was nothing but a baby, crawl out, I wouldn't eat, I wouldn't do anything, and I'd just drink a glass of water. My brother-in-law, Hugh Floyd, he tried to play alto and for a long time I never liked altos because he used to get on my nerves, but that sound, that tone he was getting, made my flesh crawl. One day I hit him with a lamp on his head. He went out and bought a gold saxophone; still couldn't play it. So we'd get into such arguments that - even as a kid
WILLIAMS

because these sounds would get into me. I'd sit at that piano, getting sounds myself, all day, and just rehearse and play. This was during the period, I guess just before I went out with anybody. It was during the time I was playing for parties. The police on their way - the police station was on the corner - they'd stop on the porch and I'd have to play a concert for them. If I was out late at night by myself, coming from a gig, they'd stop and bring me down in the patrol car to the house. They'd wait at the streetcar for me. I played concerts for them and the Hamilton Packing Company - these big trucks, you know, they'd always stop Saturdays...
In those days when you were coming home late at night, did you ever have any trouble?

None. There was always that strange protection like Margaret Warren, the police. I had a close shave a couple of times playing for parties, young boys, their parents had gone to Europe, and I just left. They were upstairs getting drunk and I ran out and left. I wouldn't tell my stepfather because he would have gone back and killed everybody, because he was very mean about things like that.
Well, we left you where you had just met John Williams. Did he join the Buzzin Harris show by himself...?
With a combo, about 6 of us including myself.
WILLIAMS
You joined his group then?...
I don't remember if I just played piano and that's all for the show. I don't remember having a drummer or anybody then.
So you were the whole thing?
I may have been. I don't remember drums or bass or tuba. See they used tubas then.
When John Williams brought his group in and you became a part of it, what was your early reaction to John? Did you like him or not like him, or what?

Not enough to (ask him) but I did it to get away from home. I admired him because he was such a giant in bringing love among musicians and bringing them together. He was such a giant in picking out problems right away and I admired him for his ability, but as far as marrying I don't think I loved him enough.
This time how long did the whole show stay together?
For a long time. We just went right to the end there, till there was nothing else more to do. They stuck together for a long time.
How wide an area did you tour?
Let's see, Indiana, Ohio - we never did hit the major cities. We were in Oklahoma, small places. It was impossible to really make a living...
How long did this go on, a couple years?
WILLIAMS
I cant remember.
It may have.
What do you remember next?

During this period we played for circuses and carnivals and that is the worst life that anybody could ever - oh, my goodness. I thought about that and I just shivered in bed once because these roustabouts - you call them that? - they are terrible... Doc Cheatham, good trumpeter, did you ever hear of him? He sounded like an [ ]. He was sensational. He was with us during that period and we played some really rough places. That's a terrible life.
When you worked a carnival what did you do for a piano?
Oh, they had a piano, there was always a piano there.
Did the carnival provide it or did you have to carry it with you?
I really don't know. No, we didn't have enough money to carry anything with us. We were just barely making it.
Speaking of Doc Cheatham, who else was in your group?

Doc Cheatham, Briscoe, and Joe Williams, a terrific guitarist. He made a banjo sound like a guitar and I loved it, because banjos - I used to hate the sound of them. He was very good. Briscoe and a drummer - I have forgotten his name completely. Later on with Seymour and Jeanette
WILLIAMS
we had Abey somebody. I can't remember his last name.
Well then eventually the Buz Harris show, the tour just came to an end?
Well, I tell you, John Williams got an offer to go with Seymour and Jeanette.
While you were still working with Buz?
Yes, and it had really petered out.
Who were Seymour and Jeanette?

One of the greatest acts on - I'll tell you, during that period you know how prejudiced they were. They wouldn't dare have a black person on Keith, Pantages, that. But Seymour and Jeanette were the only black team on Keith circuit, Pantages, and all - and Bill Bojangles. They only booked those two people. So John Williams received a wire that they needed a combo because Seymour did a strutting act and what not. He was very good at it but he had a bad heart, so he thought that if he got a small combo that would help him along. So he wired John and said he'd be making $75. Woo, that was like making a thousand dollars a week, you know! So we joined -
A week.
For how many people?
$75 each, so that was like a thousand dollars a week because we had been making $25 or $30. So we joined
WILLIAMS

Seymour and Jeanette. A strange thing happened. We came to New York - I think it was New York we had gone, either New York or Rochester, some place. So we were getting ready to rehearse. I'd always stand at the piano and look at it before I tackled it. I was just sitting there. So Seymour came out and they introduced - I don't think they introduced him to everybody. He just came out, because he was sitting there and was irritable all the time. He said, "What's that girl doing, sitting at the piano?" Nobody would say anything. He said, "Well, get her off the stage so we can play." Nobody would say anything. So I didn't move so he said, "Let's start the rehearsal." So I started playing and both of them had a fit. They didn't know that John had a woman with them. They had a fit because during this period because a woman was not really allowed to be in with a group of men or anything. They were so surprised. So he said, "We can't take her. We can't let not Keith but the manager see her because she's a black woman and we've got to put pants on her." They were wondering what they were going to do. They said, "She's good, she's good!" So John said, "Forget it; listen to her play." So we went on with that and everything was fine. About 6 months or a year later Seymour died and John Williams and the combo and I worked with Jeanette for a while till we were stranded in New York.
WILLIAMS
Stranded in New York?
Yep. We got stranded in New York and so we went back to Pittsburgh, Joe Williams, John, and I, then later on to Memphis with John. During this period is when I met Fats Waller.
When you were in New York with Seymour and Jeanette?

Yes. We had a date in the Lincoln Theatre - I imagine you've heard of the Lincoln Theatre in Harlem? Duke Ellington had just come into New York with his combo, the Washingtonians they were. They were playing the Lincoln with us because Seymour and Jeanette were the top black act. So he played on stage with the band and they had me in the pit playing with the band. Still couldn't read. I played in the band with Tricky Sam, Bubber Miley, and Sonny Greer, and then I'd go up on stage with the act. I met Fats Waller then and I can tell you he was just a sensation in New York, when they'd turn the light on people would scream, when he sat down, people would scream. I never saw such a thing. When he finished, that was the end; they had to let it cool off.
Was he playing the organ just as a solo specialty?
No.... He probably was playing for the movie but this week he did a tune before the show.
I remember someone telling me he used to play for the news reel. Nobody was watching the news reel and he did all kind of things.
Yes, he was terrific. Later on in Scranton he
WILLIAMS
was working in the Cotton Club, Connie's Inn. one Which/was in Harlem?
The Cotton Club was too.
(THIS SECTION IS NOT CLEAR)
Connie's Inn. A friend of his took me there and ...He said, "I have a little girl who can play everything you composed." Now this man was a giant. Leonard, the producer, I've forgotten his name -
Leonard Harper.

He said, "All right, Fats, we're ready for the music after you give the girl some routines." I'd say, "O.K." He'd bring out his jug and what-not and he'd say, "What's the title? What you doing?" Leonard would tell him the story. And the man would play it straight off, lyric and everything, a whole 32-bar song... So I was sitting over in the corner. This man had moved there because he was going to put them on, like a bet. He'd say, "This girl can play everything she heard you compose." "She can't!" "I bet you!" So I sat down and played. ( ) and all these other things. Fats took me and threw me up in the air. He grabbed me and threw me up in the air and he bit me and everything. I wished I wasn't even there after all that went on. I thought he was the most amazing woman's pianist, I'm going to do the same thing. What's the/name I told you my brother-in-law used to take me to hear in Pittsburgh? Lovey Austin used to write music and play with her left hand. I used to do that with Andy Kirk.
WILLIAMS
Where did you run into Lovey Austin?

I ran into Lovey Austin when I was about 8 or 9 or 10 years old. I must have been pretty small because my brother-in-law used to throw me on his shoulder if I went to sleep in the theatre, and bring me home like that. He took me up there to see her, what she was doing. She had her legs crossed, with a cigarette in her mouth, playing and writing music for the next act. When the next act came on, the music was ready. She'd pass it out to the musicians who were going to play it. So I thought, I'm going to do that one day, and I did. That's how I used to work out my arrangements with Benny Goodman, when I was with Kirk.
Why did you want to do it?

Because it was amazing, that someone could concentrate like that - play, smoke a cigarette, with her legs crossed, and playing that music... And it comes easy after once you get on to it. I always wanted to do that... because it's so creative... I think there were two people inspired me because I wanted to do what they were doing.
We're coming to the end of this reel so why don't we sort of break here.
Mary, let's get back to when you were born in Atlanta. Tell me about the circumstances of the place where you were born.
WILLIAMS

Well, I used to hear my parents speak of the land where the house was built. It seems that it was a sunken cemetery of soldiers of the Civil War and then at the time I was born - there was a midwife brought me into the world - I was born like with a veil. I guess this was a superstition but we were living in a neighborhood of a lot of superstitious people down South. This midwife told my mother that I was born with a veil over my eyes and for her to save this veil and dry it out and she could tell when I was sick and all that. I used to hear so many stories about spooks and ghosts and everything. Seemed like I picked up on that when I was about two or three years old because my mother was afraid to take me out anywhere with us. She said that one day we were walking in the field and I saw a little white dog and the white dog grew into a cow. I said, 'Come on down, Mother,' but she ran and left me but she came back. Everybody was afraid to be around me because I was seeing so many weird things.
When you saw the little white dog grow into a cow, did it?

It certainly did. I remember that. My Mother said it's amazing some of the things I used to see and some of the things I remember when I was two years old. It seems that I was playing with this little white dog
WILLIAMS
and she didn't pay any attention to it. I reached up and said, 'Oh, it's a cow,' or something like that. She ran but she said she came back and picked me up and took me home.
What did they do with the cow?

I guess it disappeared. But she said at an early age I was seeing spirits. I often wondered about a lot of other kids, you know, with their imagination. They are probably able to see them also. Because I've gone through life like that, seeing various things, except when I became Catholic - now I feel them more or less. I don't see them any more.
We'll get to that part later. But when you were saying you were seeing things and now you feel them, was this extrasensory perception?

It's a little bit of everything I guess in that direction because when I was with the Andy Kirk band my husband used to have to tie me in bed because in a hotel, a very bad hotel, I remember walking up the steps going into the hotel and I saw a man standing up at the top... with his head hanging off. I'd run or something, you know what I mean, and they'd say, there she goes again.
For example, they had to tie you in bed because otherwise what would happen?
It's like a nightmare. Whatever happened in that room, maybe a suicide or I don't know what it is, I'd see strange things from it, you know.
WILLIAMS
This kind of sense that you had, entirely aside from seeing that sort of thing and reconstructing something that happened some place, how did it affect your music?

I think that when anybody has anything like that, ESP, if you're an artist it should be put into your music, because at one time I could hear a musician playing and could hear the note he was going to make next. It was just that fast. It was just like seeing spiritual or telling someone's fortune, I knew exactly what he was going to do.
This is why you could listen to Fats Waller improvise a whole score and then you sit down and play it?

Well, I don't know, but it may have something to do with the fastness of the mind and hearing. See, when you develop a thing like that it can be good for you or it can be very bad. You can use it in a bad way, 'cause there's nothing we can do about what's happening to us. Some people lose their minds. But I think it's useful in your work.
Is this something you can control?

No, you can't control it... You see these things when you're not even expecting them. I may be walking down the street with somebody - there was a little incident when my brother-in-law was bringing me home from
WILLIAMS

a party and he carried me on his shoulder, because I had gone to sleep. That's what the men did in the family. I I was a little tired they'd just put me on their shoulder and take me home. I woke up and I said, "Don't walk into that man." He started running with me because it's a frightening thing, you know. I could see a man on the street but he couldn't see him. Once with Andy Kirk's band I grabbed the wheel because I saw an old couple on the road, passing, and the old man was crippled and passed in front of the car and /I/ grabbed the wheel... and they weren't there. I was the only person that saw it.
What would have happened, do you suppose, if you hadn't grabbed the wheel and gone right straight through what you say wasn't really there. Would there have been something there?

It could be an accident but I'm in control of that now. I've seen things while I was driving but I just kept straight through it. That happened to me not too long ago, I guess about 20 years ago, or 15. I saw a little kid run in front of the car. He was not there. Seemed like all of a sudden I thought, gosh, it's after one o'clock. There's no kid out here this size... Perhaps some little kid had got killed there.
Another thing, back in Atlanta, your mother married. Was she married before you were born or after?
WILLIAMS
She was married - I think she had left him shortly after I was born, when I was born, I'm sure, because I never met him. I only saw a picture of him.
What was his first name?
Mose Winn, W-i-n-n.
When you were younger were you Mary Lou Winn for a while?
I used Winn and I used Burley for the last name. I was Mary Louise Winn and I used Burley.
Did you use them interchangeably...?

I just mixed them up. Often when someone was interviewing me I said Mary Lou Winn and I'd say Mary Lou Burley. One time I said Mary Louise Winn Burley, until Jack Kapp with the Decca, changed my name to Mary Lou Williams. Well, I had married John Williams, so he changed my name to Mary Lou Williams.
Up until that point had you ever called yourself professionally Mary Lou Williams?
No, never. Jack Kapp did this.
We'll get to the Andy Kirk part. You never, when you sat in with the Andy Kirk band, you were never Mary Lou Williams then?
No.
Were you anything consistent...?
Burley. In some of the old write-ups you'd see Mary Lou Winn Burley, or Mary Lou Winn.
WILLIAMS
But there wasn't a period in which you stopped being Mary Lou Winn and became Mary Lou Burley?
Yes, before I was named Williams, before I got married. I stuck to the Burley because I was very fond of my stepfather, Fletcher Burley.
That's when you dropped the Winn?
Yes.
O.K., now, we left you in New York and that's Jelly Roll Morton? when you met Fats Waller. Was that when you met John Williams?
I met John Williams while I was with the Buzzy Harris show.
No, I said Jelly Roll Morton.

Before I joined the Buzzin' Harris show somebody brought me to New York for a visit, some musical person. I was playing so much of Jelly Roll Morton until somebody took me to his office... I was not with the band or anything.
And that was when you played the Pearls' for him?
Yes.
I see, and you were told that was not the way to play it?
In a very rough way.
Did you play some of your own things for him then too?
WILLIAMS

No, I was only interested in him. I don't think I was writing too much then. I was just playing things that I heard or people were teaching me new tunes or things like that. I didn't start to write until I was with Andy Kirk.
Now, after New York you went back to Pittsburgh and then you went to Memphis?

I went to Memphis after Seymour died. We went with Seymour and Jeanette, his wife, for a while and we were stranded, as I said, and finally made it to Pittsburgh. Joe Williams - I left him there with my people, the guitar and banjo player.
Had you married John Williams at that time?
No, we got married in Memphis.
Was Joe related to John?

No, but they went to school together. Joe Williams was from Kansas City, Kansas; and John was from Memphis, Tennessee, but he went to school in Kansas City. That's where he met Joe. When we went to Memphis, Tennessee, that's where John Williams my husband - who later became my husband - was born and so we got in the band together. He was such a terrific man. The union musicians there - they had no union when I was there - he got a union going for them. The musicians would work like from 8 o'clock till 3 or 4 in the morning and they'd get
WILLIAMS 39

paid $2, so John, when he left Memphis they were making over $20-25 and the leader $30, because I remember once - they were very, very prejudiced in Memphis - he had such a terrific band and Jimmy Lunceford was teaching at a high school there. He and Jimmy Lunceford were very good friends (John Williams and Jimmy Lunceford). So everything that John did Jimmy would try to do something better. So he said to John, "I'm going to get a band better than that combo you have." Jimmy got himself a girl piano player and he taught kids - high school pupils, he was teaching in a high school - he taught them music. All these young kids being brought up in Memphis, he taught them music. He and John used to play checkers and John would beat him playing checkers and he'd say, "That's all right; I'm going to get a band better than you."

So I worked there for a while. Being in the North so long I was pretty mean to get along with because I wasn't used to what was happening. Before John got his combo I got a little job out on the outskirts of Memphis and these people were ringing a bell and saying, "I want this," and telling me, "You're from the North and if you don't do what we want you to do... yeah, we'll lynch you" and this guy took me home every night, he was talking all this talk and I waited till I got in front of the house and started screaming and so... (LAUGHTER)
Were you playing solo?
WILLIAMS
Yes, by myself. I worked for Mrs. Singleton and it was a bad night club, you know, where they gambled and everything. Mrs. Singleton owned this club.
Was she related to Zutty?

No, no relation. This was in Memphis. One night I went to sleep on the street car. Usually when you sat in the front and it began to get crowded with whites you had to move to the back. I was sleeping so when we got out to the end of the street car line the conductor said, "You're going to be hurt, little girl, because you're supposed to move in the back." I said, "I went to sleep." When the car made the last stop I started screaming on him and scratching him. I didn't understand this, you know. I worked for Mrs. Singleton about a year and a half till I had to leave because a farmer came in from Mississippi and had paid the black cook $50 to kidnap me and take me down to Mississippi. You wouldn't have heard from me any more because that had happened to many, many younger people in Memphis. They'd take them to in Mississippi, man and you'd have to go through each town to get back to Memphis and they'd stop you on the way. So Mrs. Singleton had me go home and wait till this guy left. He stayed around Memphis for 2 weeks trying to get me down to Mississippi.
Was Mrs. Singleton black?
WILLIAMS 41

She was white. She was very nice and kind. She also had a little young kid that it seemed that the family had died out or something and left her with a little young boy and he was about 15 years old. She was as nice as she could be to him. She was very kind but I didn't like some of the other people that was there.
You worked there for about a year?

Well, just about 6 months or so because/She I had to leave - wouldn't trust me - I mean wouldn't... because of conditions that existed like that in Tennessee. So what happened, John got this terrific combo going out at the White Rose or something like that. in Memphis. We were just doing real great and all of a sudden wo decided to join Andy Kirk's band. So I had to get someone to play with me to take his place so I hired Jimmy Lunceford. He worked /with me for about 6 months and this was while we were in Memphis.
What became of Jimmy's band...?
Jimmy didn't have his band. It wasn't organized. He didn't organize it until maybe about 6 months or a year after I left Memphis.
It wasn't Andy Kirk that John was going to join?
No. J. Holder
It seemed that was kind of a reckless guy with money and he'd done this so many times so that the entire band called a meeting and they decided to have Andy as the leader of the band...
WILLIAMS
This happened after you had joined?
After I had joined. Jimmy Lunceford worked for me for about, I guess, 6 months, I don't know how long it was...
Why did you stay that long in Memphis after John left?

Because he had built up such a big clientele with all the gigs and jobs and things that he had worked for - I guess we were there 2 or 3 years. They still wanted some parts of the band - he was missing and I was a big part of it, being so tiny and whatnot, and then we had some dates that we had to play. We had to finish these dates. We got some more dates then to play.
I see. So you led the band and finished those up? Then was that when you went to Oklahoma City?

Yes, drove to Oklahoma City, changed tires and everything. His mother was with me. A little old car that John had, a Chevrolet, looked like a bathtub. I have a picture of it now and I laugh about it. I drove from Memphis to Oklahoma.
How far is that?
I guess about 600 miles.
How long did it take you, do you know?
I don't remember. I know we had flat tires and everything on the way.
Who changed the tires?
WILLIAMS

Oh, I did. I changed the tires and I'd fix them up. Roland Mayfield, you know, the man who used to pick me up in Pittsburgh, taught me how to drive and how to fix cars and everything. My brother-in-law helped and if anything was wrong with any of those cars I could fix it myself. His mother was with me. It was like being on a desert, all the turtle-back roads, sand, dirt roads, you know. So we finally made it there and got in all right. See Roland taught me how to - I used to race when I was 10 or 12 years old. He taught me how to race and all that, do tricks in the car.
So we got into Oklahoma City. After I arrived, the boys were dissatisfied about T. Holder and they called a meeting -
Did you join the band to play?

No, I was there as John's wife but he was very shrewd about it. He had his way of working me in. The pianist was very, very great but not as exciting. He was more of a - how shall I say it? - legit pianist, very beautiful chords and very wonderful pianist. So what I did was to go out on trips with them and when they were stuck - I'd sit in the instrumental truck, I'd drive a car or the instrumental truck or something - and if they got stuck and weren't going over big they'd call me in to do "Froggy Bottom" or something.
WILLIAMS
Were you doing "Froggy Bottom" by then?

Well, there were other tunes similar to that, but "Froggy Bottom" later, about a year later it was written. Before we even recorded it, you know. So we did this for quite a while and I traveled with the band and I'd sit in and play with him. After we played Oklahoma City, played one-nighters and all down through the Indian Territory. This was very exciting for me. We decided to leave. One thing I wanted to tell you - there was the most handsome - the boys were the most handsome guys and the most wonderful gentlemen that I've ever met. I don't think any one of them was over 25 or 26 years old but they were so well trained. Most of them were college graduates or something and they dressed very fine and they were so respectful of people. I've never been around a group like that, of musicians.
How had T. Holder managed to get this group together, especially...?

I really don't know. I never did find out but it was something really special. Claude Williams had played the violin and he was terrific. This was the most wonderful thing how they rehearsed. They'd call a rehearsal and nobody would prepare an arrangement. They'd do it while they were there. In one corner somebody would be playing cards or talking or something and Andy would say, "O.K.,
WILLIAMS

rhythm section first." And after that the trumpets and the saxophones. In this particular band they had a guy that played - they called him like a clown. He did all the acrobatics and everything on his back with this tenor and all that. They had other musicians that were real true musicians and what I did when I began writing, I'd teach this guy how to phrase with them because he was a little corny - the one that was doing all the tricks while he was playing. They did little acts and they did everything. They could play like Guy Lombardo and they could swing like Count Basie. It was the most amazing band I've ever been with in my life. They could play so many different styles and this put them in the category of Guy Lombardo. They could play for proms and everything and then go to an all black dance and be just as good, you know, swinging.
They worked a lot of white dates?

Yes, they did more white dates than anything else. Then when we first began to hit in the 30's everyone thought Andy was white because they had never seen a picture of him, because the band sounded like it on some things that we played. He believed in phrasing ballads in a very beautiful way, like violins. This band, they had a way of getting arrangements and things on the spot. During that era we didn't have great readers among black musicians and these guys could read anything. Like the first trumpet had such a sound, Big Jim Lawson, he was terrific.
WILLIAMS

Maybe the other two trumpets or one trumpet sound wasn't as big and he just covered the entire band sometimes when we didn't have everybody with a good sound. It was a most enjoyable thing after I joined them. It was exciting and I think they are really the reasons that I began to arrange.
How long after you and John went to Oklahoma City did Andy take over the band?

I think it was a matter of about 3 months because I remember going to their first rehearsal and the next 2 or 3 was a meeting when they decided to get rid of Teholder because he had gambled away their salary for that week and he had been doing that all along.
Once Andy took over the band did you play more? Was there any difference in - ?
I didn't play with that band - now that must have been around 1928, '27 or '28. I didn't join the band until '31 and all this time I was traveling and on one-nighters and everything with them.
Driving a bus?
Driving everything.
What else did they have besides a bus?
They didn't have a bus. We had a fleet of cars. The boys had bought the instrumental truck that carried the instruments.
You drove that too?
WILLIAMS
Once or twice. I'd drive John's car, the Chevrolet.
How wide an area did the band cover then?

All through Oklahoma, even to Mississippi, Arkansas, and Colorado. Let's see; they went even to as far as - we didn't go all the way to California then, but we went some peculiar places that I never dreamed of being: Peoria, Illinois - just little small towns, you know.
At this time where was your home base, in Oklahoma City?
It was in Oklahoma.
Do you mean the state or the city?
No, the city, the city of Oklahoma. We worked in Tulsa maybe 3 or 4 months during the summer season and then we'd go back to Oklahoma.
When did the band get into Kansas City?

The band got into Kansas City I think about 2 years after John Williams joined it. There was an opening at the Playmore there in Kansas, I think it was the Playmore, and Andy decided to go there. After that Kansas City became the headquarters for the band.
Once the band got to Kansas City, was that when you started to write.
Yes, write. Andy knew that I had ideas - I was writing all along but I couldn't write it down. I'd give them
WILLIAMS

ideas during the rehearsal. Maybe they wanted to play a song like "Singing in the Rain" and I'd say, "Well, listen to this." Andy would take it down real fast but sometimes they didn't at all. In Kansas City he'd come to the house like 10 o'clock in the morning and sit there till 12. I said, I can't go through this, so after about 2 weeks or a week or so he came down and I had an arrangement ready for him. The only thing that wasn't really balanced right was the tenor and the trombones and he showed me that. From that day on I began writing.
Were you just doing this from instinct then, the writing?
I watched him. I can learn a lot through watching. That was my bag, see, watching people and doing what they do.
All this period, this two years when you're traveling with the band and just occasionally getting to play, how did you feel? Did you feel that you were going anywhere?

No, it wasn't that; I thought I was helping. There's a peculiar thing about me in life. You know if you want to really hear me play or write something, give me somebody to help. If I think that I'm helping a situation, somebody say, Mary come out to the church and do something and help us and do this - it's amazing the work that I can
WILLIAMS

do and I'm very happy with my work. That's been my bag since I've been born. If I think I'm helping someone I get great things going and I was helping them in a way. I discovered chords and Andy used to say to me, "You can't do that. It's against the rules of writing music." I said, "But I hear a sixth in this chord." He said, "But you can't do it." I said, "I'm going to do it." I did the arrangement of, before I did "Walkin'", trumpet and 3 saxophones. We only had 3 saxophones and one trumpet and trombone, something like that. So what I did, I put a trumpet in and I had 3 saxophones to play 4-part harmony. He kept telling me it was against the rules of the chord. In that year I guess it was but I was hearing - I found these things on the piano and I said, this will sound good - it sounds good here. After a while I started arranging it.
How did you happen to become a regular member of the band?

Well, we scuffled. Let's see, we went to the Savoy in New York. By this time we were playing "Froggy Bottom" and things like that. They called me in to sing because Chick Webb was really blasting town with all bands and they were getting rid of all bands that came in there. I guess you heard about that era; it was sensational. When he came in you just prayed that you'd go over.
WILLIAMS
So they called for me and I'd be out in the car, I'd be downstairs playing miniature golf, and I'd go up and break it up, 'cause I was so tiny.
Mary, if you all these years have been breaking it up on this basis of being called in specially, why did they never put you on a regular basis?

Well, because they had this pianist. They respected him. Jack was a nice guy. Number one, Jack - I don't know his name - Jack Somebody. He was a good man and everything. It may have been that they didn't want a woman in the band because women during that era was not playing with men. That was another thing that made people scream and carry on, because they saw a woman and one that weighed 90 pounds. My feet was just barely touching the floor. That was a good point about it, but to hear me play so heavy like a man, that was something else. I don't know why John wasn't pushing it but he was through. He was putting me like, you know, in position. He had me on the scene. But I tell you what happened. We worked with Blanche Calloway in Philadelphia. This was before I joined the band. Whenever they went on tours I was with them. We went to Philadelphia; we worked for the Steeple there. You've heard about that. They were Ethel Waters, Bill Bailey -
This is the Pearl Theatre?
Pearl Theatre, we were working at the Pearl Theatre
WILLIAMS

in Philadelphia. Andy decided to use me for that theatre date, so he put me on a little miniature piano and had Jack on a big Steinway. So I was on the left of it, a left-handed stage, and he was over to the right. One afternoon Jack got sick or something happened to him. Steeple used to bring people in - he said, "Call the kid." He had the people sitting in the theatre just listening to me play and all that but they wouldn't do anything about Jack. Yes.

When did you first meet Thelonious Monk?

I think it was the year of 1930 in Kansas City. He was traveling with a show somewhat like a medicine show. The music was so great in Kansas City so he stopped off there. They had opened up a new night club called the Subway or something like that in Kansas City and I met Monk there and he was playing the same way he plays now. No one understood it. I used to hang out with him and we became great friends then. During that period Lester Young, Herschel Evans, and Count Basie and all the musicians used to go down to the Subway to hear Monk play.
What happened to music in Kansas City because of Monk?

I don't think the music changed too much as far as Monk was concerned. Everybody in Kansas City you must remember were playing different sounds, you know. They were playing in their own individual styles.
WILLIAMS 84

Like we had one pianist - I think I mentioned that to you once before - his name was Sleepy. His eyes were half closed and he played exactly like Art Tatum in all the difficult keys like F sharp, B natural, A natural. What was great as far as the scene of Kansas City was, that all these various styles and everybody was so original.
Was this true of all the musicians or are you speaking primarily -
Practically all the musicians. No one ever copied anybody else. That was really unique, you know, as far as Kansas City. We had the Cherry Blossom where we used to go and jam.
Where was the Cherry Blossom?

Oh goodness, I've forgotten the street. I think 18th and Vine. This was where they had a floor show and everything but after the floor show everybody would jam I guess from 1 o'clock till maybe 12 the next day. We had a wonderful friend that used to help out the musicians. He and Piney Brown were really friends of the musicians. He was known by the name of Country and he worked for a judge there, Judge Gershon. We used to laugh about the two of them together. Country was the chauffeur and Judge Gershon's right-hand man. Whenever anybody got into trouble Country would - these two were the most comical act you've ever seen, whether in the movies or anything. Whenever one of the musicians had gotten into trouble his case
WILLIAMS 85

would come up in court and Gershon would say, "So-and-so blabla," whatever his name was and Country would sneak out the door. He'd say, "Come back here, Country. I know what you've done." See the musician didn't appear and Country had gone out to where he was jailed and told that Judge Gershon said to turn him loose. It was a big political town anyway and he did things like that and the Judge would come down 18th Street - I saw him myself. It happened to be around 3 o'clock and he'd look in all the pool halls and all the restaurants and everything, asking for Country and Country was hiding underneath the pool table. Country was a fabulous and fine-looking tall black man. He was just handsome. He was hiding under this pool table and Gershon was walking up and down 18th Street looking for him. He'd say, "Don't tell him where I am." He'd gotten drunk all night and had lost his voice and everything, so Gershon said, "I'm looking for Country. Do you know what he did?" Country had pawned two tires on his Cadillac. He'd carry on with the musicians and buy drinks and do things for them so this particular night he pawned these two tires and the car was hiked up on one side without any tires on it. That was really funny, what happened with him. Let's see, something else happened.
Did musicians in Kansas City get in trouble a lot? Were they -
No, no, not in trouble. I'll tell you what happened a couple of times. Kansas City was really prejudiced
WILLIAMS

when I first went there, about the streetcar, the blacks sitting in the back but in a matter of a year that was cleared up. What really happened was that they'd probably be in the house drinking with white and black. This was during Prohibition and I remember 3 or 4 of our boys got picked up like that. They were sitting drinking with - there was two white girls and the others were the boys in the band. About 3 of the boys out of the band was just sitting there drinking. We used to jam and do things like that and the girls would come around to hear it. It so happened that one of the girls was married or was a girl friend to a big detective there and he'd been peeping under the curtain all the time they were in the house. So he went away and brought the wagon back and arrested all of them but it didn't stand up at all because some of them was released before Country even came into the picture because the law is that black and white could be in the same house drinking and there was no need to arrest them if no one had taken their coats off. That was a peculiar law. They had just arrived in the house and this detective happened to follow his girl friend and saw her. He was peeping under the curtain and Salty Dog, somebody like that, ran in the house. A guy by the name of Salty Dog told the guys that this detective was outside but it was too late then. He called the police and picked them up.
WILLIAMS
Just little things like that. They didn't get into big trouble and whatever they did it was just like they hadn't because Country would release them.
You say after about a year though the white and black thing got straightened out?

Oh, yes, it wasn't very long because I think I arrived in Kansas City, to really live there, in '29 or '30 and I was too busy with music to pay much attention to anything but it disappeared quite fast.
Did whites come down to the black clubs?

Yes, whites came everywhere; that's the reason why the guys got into trouble. They were always in the black district. Count Basie and I had about 30 pupils between us, that we were teaching to play jazz.
And they were white?
Yes, they were white.
Did you have black pupils too?
Oh sure, we had both, but we had more whites than anything else.
Was there any jazz in the white sections of town in Kansas City?

There was jazz clubs. My attention was focused where the giants were and that was 18th and Vine or 12th Street. We had many white musicians that came there, mostly out of the city, like Ben Pollack and those people like that.
WILLIAMS
When they were traveling through?
Yes.
Where did they usually play?
Oh, the Muhlenbach Hotel was a popular place for them there. I think that was the only one that they played.

Stumpy Buddy was a terrific trombonist...
About Lucille and Louise?

They put them in the music scene because they followed all the musicians. They were crazy about musicians but they were two beautiful girls and I think their father was a big political leader and a wonderful Italian man off of Fifth Avenue. Fifth Avenue was a pretty rough street; after jam sessions certain nights we'd all go there. Lucille and Louise were not allowed out, not unless their mother asked me if I was going along with them. I don't know why she thought I could protect them. They were both older than what I was by 2 years. There was another friend of mine - Louise, Lucille, and Rosita (Shewing,) I'm telling you they was something else. I didn't have one chance to sit in on a jam session after we went out together because the whole town practically was destroyed. These two little girls (I think they were between 18 and 20 years old), they'd go in a night club and if they took a couple of drinks or so, they'd just take the pictures off the wall. Sammy Price happened to be playing in the club one night and he was a

terrific boogie-woogie pianist and they always liked to go to see him. Rough in what way, Mary Lou?

Why did they make him work without pay?
If you angered them their temper was terrible. If you angered them in any way.
What was the pay like then in Kansas City?

I don't think it was very much. I hadn't joined the band then. I heard that Count Basie had to work either one or two weeks without pay. Andy Kirk's band went in next and we had a singer with us and he got in a dispute with one of the gangsters there. The gangster looked at

him and he says, "Andy, if it wasn't for you I'd kill him!"

Oh, sure he meant it, sure. We worked for the Gershwin brothers.

No, nothing rubbed off on me. I think music was such a great thing that you could hit me on top of the head and I wouldn't know. All I did was just stay up nights, days and nights, playing. Right.

Just beautiful. She reminded me of - what was the girl from Paris? Josephine Baker, that type.

That doesn't seem to make sense. Man!
