Dick Wilson stuck his head out and said, "Man, go ahead now because we're going to jam." We stayed there and went back the next day. We didn't care what he did because during that era everybody was just thirsting to play. You just had to play someplace. There was another club, private club, we opened up when Don Byas was with us on the jam session. It was a private club and there was about 3 people in this club when we first started jamming there. The place became packed and jammed. One night we went to jam and they wouldn't let us in.
Where was that club?
At 118th and Seventh Avenue?
Did it have a name?
No, I don't know the name of it.
Were you at Minton's quite a bit too?
Every night.
How did it work out if Monk - did everybody take turns on the piano or -
Yes, they had the same idea that Kansas City had, you know. Several pianists were there and they'd take turns.
I heard stories about musicians coming up from downtown and trying to find out what was happening.
WILLIAMS
They did and they would write music on their cuffs, on toilet paper, and everything.
Did they try to sit in?
No, they didn't try to sit in. They were trying to get the phrasing of it so Monk and the cats said, "What's the use? We just have to try to get on out downtown and try to get a job."
How about some of the older black musicians? Did they sit in too?
Well, I only saw Dizzy there and I think Roy Eldridge and, who else?
I heard stories of Fats Waller.

I never saw Fats there but I wasn't there all the time. I was there maybe about a year, six months, I don't remember just how long, but I've never seen any of the older musicians. In fact I lost the friendship of a lot of older musicians by hanging out with the young musicians.
Why?
It created a jealousy. When bop came along they felt that it was so strange that it wasn't right, that it wasn't good. You know, you always have that dissension.
Was it that they didn't understand it?
They didn't understand it and it was so far out. I understand that a lot of musicians were in the Army. When they came out and heard that, they put their instruments
WILLIAMS 103
down and got a job working. They thought maybe the music was too tough to play.
Why did you have no trouble going along with it?

Because most of them needed inspiration and they wrote the music up here at the house. I had a white carpet here on the floor. We used to sit on this carpet. I kept it clean, you know. We ate on it and did everything. Tadd Dameron and all the cats used to come. Monk used to come here and write his music. I have some music he left here now - and Bud. If they wrote at home they'd bring it here for me to hear it and see how I liked it.
How long have you had this carpet?

Since '41, 32 years. Very famous house. Mel Torme used to come here, Sarah Vaughan, even Leonard Feather, Benny Goodman. Seemed like it was more inspiration for them than I had out of the house. I had to go down to Nola's and get my inspiration. Dizzy, Miles - oh, just all the musicians came here. Seemed like I was inspiration or something for them.
As you came into the period when bop was happening, were you dissatisfied with the older music or did you happen to like it?

I was dissatisfied completely with the older music. I was working at the Cafe downtown and I was late so many times that Barney fired me when I went uptown. I was so happy when he fired me. I said to John Castle,
WILLIAMS 104

"Oo, I got fired!" I was talking to Thelma Carpenter and somebody /said, "Where are you working?" "I don't know, I got fired." Thelma said, "You shouldn't do that." in New York. You wouldn't get another job." I said, "I'd rather be out." I was up there playing real commercial music and skipping notes on classical - the worse you played it the better you'd go over - and the worst commercial music. I was hanging out on 52nd Street where Billie Holiday was. I heard this music and it was terrific. Barney did hire me back. He wanted me back and I stayed a short time, but the music was so beautiful it just gave you a sight of a new picture happening in the jazz. It had such a beautiful feeling. It didn't take me very long to get on to it or create in my own way from it, for certain things that had happened.
When you say you seem to have been an inspiration to all these people that came up here, in what way were you an inspiration. Was it that you gave them ideas?

Well, sometimes I did Tadd Dameron when he'd get stuck in his arrangement like me or any other arranger. He'd come up and I'd say, "Get out of it this way." I'd play it on the piano or if he didn't like that I'd play a record. I get my inspiration from modern classical things. I get in a mood, you know, to write. I always have used that as inspiration for writing.
Play records of modern classical things?
WILLIAMS
stack of them.

Delius or Schönberg. I have a lot of don't ask me to name it all - in the closet. After a while a musician knew what I was doing and he stole them. I've got for about 5 copies of Schönberg, you know, when he did - well, I can't remember names, but it was very inspiring to write music. I'd either do that or play something or help him with the arrangement.
But in order to get yourself in the mood, you played records, is that right?
Sometimes. Often if I was feeling good I'd just sit on down and play some things and see if he liked it.
Even when you were writing new things, did you sometimes reach into your own past to get ideas?

No. I tell you what it happensa. It would just come right out. You may be walking down the street and it comes out of the sky. But there's other times when you don't feel like writing or you're just dry. I would never take a job as an arranger or creative artist because you can run dry and you just have to leave it alone for 6 months, 4 to 6 months. Sometimes riding on the subway would inspire me, the clicking of the wheels, to write something. But there are times when everything is completely gone as if you've never written anything and nothing happens at all.
A dry spell. You say you wouldn't take a job as a creative artist, what are you doing - ?
WILLIAMS 106
I mean as an arranger or writer, that's what I mean, because I'm too creative. I have to wait for an inspiration.
But every time you sit down to play you've been creative.
Yes, it's better for me that way. I can create much better if the bass player's with me, if he doesn't interfere.
Now, want to stop a minute?
Let's go back to Pittsburgh where you were brought up.

Yes, I was in grade school. I can tell you about this wonderful principal we had, Miss Milholland. It was a white school and all white teachers. She had a deep something for black kids and black people. She was the most beautiful woman I've ever seen. I think she was about 6 feet something - she was very tall. If she discovered a talented black person she'd do everything in her power to help them. I think I was supposed to be in school - I was only in the third grade now. I was supposed to be in school at 9 o'clock. She'd give me until 9:30 or 10 to get in. She was booking me on gigs over at Tech University. She'd take me home with her and have me play for everybody in the place where she lived. She just was so beautiful.
WILLIAMS 107

What really happened - I used to hide under the bed. I don't know if I told you about this and I think it's a terrible thing that anybody would indoctrinate a black kid against what happened to them when they were in slavery, what happened to their parents when they were in slavery, because it affected me so when I was quite young. I was in the third grade, I remember. I usedto hide under the bed and listen to my great-grandparents talk about slaves and things. It infuriated me so that when I went to school I hit my teacher, Miss Itzel, with a stick. I just walked in school and hit her with a stick.
Why?

I said, "You hate black people and I hate white people," something like that. So Miss Itzel said, "This poor child," and she bought me dolls and candy and everything and Miss Milholland heard about it. They discovered I had perfect pitch and she did everything about instruments and a lot of things - she's so talented she can play all the instruments. She had a music store to send all the instruments out to me and I played violin and the teacher got rid of me fast. He says to them, "You better not bother her because already she's playing "The Sheik" on one string." You just leave her alone and let her find out her own music and find out what she's going to do." As I said before, Miss Milholland would book me over for afternoon teas at
WILLIAMS
the Tech University and other little gigs. That's the reason why I think it's very bad in telling a child about anything that has happened in the past against any race of people.
In your case it wasn't the school that was telling you this, this was overheard in your home?

This was overheard. You see, my great-grandparents were born I guess about a year after the slaves were freed. They were both very fair, my grandmother especially. My grandfather had blonde hair. She used to tell how they used to put them out in the sun and try to parch them black because they were very, very fair and my grandmother is too. I'd hear them tell all these tales and about the slaves and what had happened. It really angered me and I can understand what's happened to the young black kids of today, because they really shouldn't - they should find out the history but they shouldn't hear too many things because they start thinking wrong. But eventually
When you say they shouldn't hear about the history, you mean they should get the whole -
The whole history.
The whole and not just pieces of it.
And especially they should get the history of black Americans. I think that's really what they need now.
You say the school was a white school that you went to?
WILLIAMS 109
Yes, it was an all white school.
All white except you?

No, they had Italians and black people and Irish and everybody going to the school. I think they had more Italians and blacks than any other race. This particular school, when I was going, I guess I was about 12 years old when I met Roland Mayfield - you know he's a big part of my life in music because he did everything to help. He used to buy cars and things and he allowed the girls - he taught all of us how to drive and how to race and how to do a lot of things.
How to race?
Yes. I used to race cars but it was in the city, on the Bigelow Boulevard.
What kind of races were they?

Just racing. Somebody would come up and bump the back of your car and it meant they wanted to race. When I was 12 years old he taught me how to fix a car. I was a mechanic; I could fix cars. There was a man on his way to meet my aunt in Philadelphia and he took us to Philadelphia. Margaret Warren, the girl I told you about that protected us when we were out with the show - she was a dancer - was riding along with us and he walked back about a mile to the garage and I drove the car in. The men there laughed because I had fixed the car. Roland taught me how
WILLIAMS 110

to do that. When Earl Hines gave his little dances in Pittsburgh - I think he was about 6 or 7 years older than any of us - they had a tough gang from downtown come out and try to break up the dances, fight, and they did a little bit of everything - Soho gang. When Roland stepped out, the street car wasn't going fast enough for them to jump on the street car and try to get away because he'd break up the gangs and everything. He was a terrific man.
Do you want to get into the Buck and Bubbles?

The bands, when they came to Pittsburgh they'd drive in to my little street on (Wehnwood) street and pick me up and take me out on gigs with them, during the period when the bands used to come to Pittsburgh. By this time I was known as the little piano girl. Everybody called me that and Roland Mayfield had gotten a special made (Ford?) Chrysler with a 4-gear shift on it and he'd given me this car. My mother said, 'Roland is crazy.' I was going to school. He'd come to school, park the car, walk back and get in one of these other cars. He had about 3 or 4 cars. I'd drive down to a night club - I think that was also called the Subway - on Wiley Avenue. My mother never knew I was going down there because Wiley Avenue was so rough. It was so tough that they said one night a guy got on the street car and took over and threw the motorman off. During this period Buck and Bubbles - Buck was a terrific pianist
WILLIAMS
and nobody knew that. He came to town -
Didn't he play piano in the act, though?
Yes, he played piano and was terrific, a style that you never heard before. The swing part of it equaled Fats Waller. It was terrific.
WILLIAMS 112

During the period when the bands used to come to Pittsburgh I met Buck. He was a great pianist but I don't think many musicians knew it because he had that comedy act going with Bubbles. He'd come to Pittsburgh and he'd say, "Now I'm going to teach you some of my things." Buck was a great teacher for me. We'd be in the Subway jamming and he'd say, "Hey, look, girl, you like me. Come over here. I'm going to teach you something." He showed me runs. Later on after I met Count Basie and Art Tatum, Buck showed me a run that Art Tatum - it was his famous run. He made it from top to bottom and Buck had taught me that run. He said, "Now when you get in front of Count Basie and Art Tatum, you make it like this," and he turned it around. One night I was jamming with Art. Art played and I was playing so I played this run that Buck had taught me and Art Tatum said, "Hey, what's that? Play it again." For about 3 or 4 years he and Count Basie were making this run the wrong way. That's the type of musician Buck was. He'd show me something but he didn't want me to play it when they were around, 'cause he didn't want them to learn it. They came around and would hear me turn it around and make it some other way.
Was there a lot of jealousy around then?
There was jealousy all during all my period. It was mostly around women. I remember once when I was with
WILLIAMS

Buzzin the Buzz and Harris show. We were traveling and it seems I was so tiny that - I said to you once before that one of the musicians grabbed me and threw me up in the air, just grabbed me and kissed me and kissed me. The reason I'm afraid of a knife, someone pulls a knife out I'll faint almost, because our trumpet player's wife happened to be around and when he did that, she pulled a razor out on me. I was nothing but a little girl. I became so frightened. Then her husband put me down and she hit me. I accidentally knocked her out because I was warding off her blows. That frightened me and I fainted.

One other time that I ran into something like that, my husband was very tall, handsome ladies' man and he was always teasing. He had one girl in Tulsa, Oklahoma, thinking that he was going to marry her, but his wife wouldn't allow it. I knew nothing about it and the wives were protecting me in the Andy Kirk band and I didn't know it. Bessie Lawson and Ophie Harrington and Mabel Durham and a couple of the girls, they lived across the street from me and when I got out to go to the store or anything I noticed they'd come out of the house and go to the store with me. He'd met one of the natives down there and she was very, very jealous of him. He was kidding around with her and she was trying to kill me. She was thinking that maybe I wouldn't give him a divorce to marry her. She was more in love with him than he was with her.
WILLIAMS 114
Did you ever run into her?

No, I never saw her. They said she was a blonde girl, something, I don't know. They described her to me but I never even went looking for her. I was so dumb, so full of music till they called me "Dummy". I never paid attention to any danger or anything else. There was always music around, but later on I discovered that the wives were protecting me and they often would protect me. There was quite a bit of jealousy around. With this Buz ZIN Harris thing, his wife was very jealous of me and one day he hit her in the eye. We happened to be out in the country and he walked around a cow all day because he said something like that if you put it on the eye it's like a raw steak. He was walking to get something to heal her eye.
Anything else you can tell us?

I guess plenty of things. I can't think of anything right now... Ben Webster in Kansas City, I met him. Did I tell you about him? He came from a very wealthy wonderful family of doctors and lawyers and teachers, but he lived right around the corner from 12th Street, a pretty rough street where all the night clubs were. They said when Ben Webster was 15 or 16 years old his parents were putting $75, $100, $50 suits on him then. He was called little Peck's Bad Boy because they couldn't keep him in college. He'd been sent to several colleges. One day Ben was telling
WILLIAMS 115

us a story. He said the girls were dressing in the dormitory and he was peeping through the window and fell through the window. He had a cut on his arm. But he was a terrific tenor man and Ben Webster was really my first love. We used to be together all the time. I loved him. Things that he did in the band would shame the boys and after he was with us about a year he was just as nice and calm, because the guys were so nice in the band and they always helped wild musicians like Ben and he was really a wild one.
But he was your first love and nothing ever came of it?
No, no, no. He was really a wild man and he was really too wild for me.
Do you want to stop and check your notes again?
Mildred Bailey.

Yes, I recorded with her. She was a great favorite of John Hammond's, you know. Mildred asked me to do an engagement with her at the 18th Hole on 52nd Street, so that's where we were in the summer of '52 with George Auld's band. It was a terrific engagement except Mildred used to become disturbed. There was a girl that used to be in New York - Stella Brooks, did you ever hear of her? Stella Brooks was a very good singer and very good actress.
WILLIAMS 116

I loved her and she's a very good friend of mine, but Stella had something going in her that used to disturb all the singers including Sarah and Billie Holiday. Once they asked Billie Holiday, "Do you like Stella Brooks' singing?" Billie Holiday said, "She can't even blow her nose." Because Stella with her bad ways had angered so many singers at things until they disliked her. This one engagement Mildred just couldn't sing one night and I asked her what was wrong. She said, "Mary, get her out, get her out. She came here to see you. Get her out. I can't sing. She's out there making faces..." Stella was so funny when she came around.
Why did she bother singers? What did she do to singers?

I don't know, something happened with singers. No, she didn't bother me because I played piano, but there was something - Stella was a very beautiful person, you could have a ball with her, but she didn't like anybody much, you know what I mean, when they were playing or anything. I guess she didn't bother me because she thought one day I'd be accompanying her on piano but I would be afraid to work for her. I loved Stella; Stella was very nice. I used to hang out with Mildred. I'd go down to her house and this particular morning she was just sick about the whole thing because I couldn't get Stella to leave. She sat there and made catcalls and everything
WILLIAMS
while Mildred was singing. She used to do the same thing to Billie but not for long.
Was Mildred a rather unhappy person when you knew her?

She didn't seem to be unhappy when I was around her but I heard she was, because I'd go to her place and we'd get into music. She was always so jolly. I also heard she was difficult to get along with but I got along with her.
Was this when she split up with Red Norvo?

Yes, this was when she split up with him. She was with him when I first met her and they had had a dispute or something. It happened one morning when I went to see her. But we'd go all up in Harlem and everything. Andy Kirk had a barbecue place and she ordered barbecued chili and so many different things and got sick that night and said the food was no good. The next time she went up there Andy said to her, 'Well, if you eat as much as you eat, you will get sick.'
She had to do something to keep her figure.

Right. A little later on I went into another club on 52nd Street. I think (Mavis Irvin) Levy owned this place, you know, it was part of Birdland. What had really happened, Birdland brought all the bop modern musicians out - Charlie Parker and all of them. Max Roach, Bud Powell, and some
WILLIAMS 118
of them would come to me and ask my advice about things.
Why were you doing this?

I don't know what happened because see I was working on the East Side and various places out of the city, but when I got this job I was alternating with Billy Taylor. I can't remember the name of this place, at 52nd and Eighth Avenue. So I had a way of always helping musicians. At one time I was recording for Moe Asch and what happened, he was expecting a pianist and I had taken Bill Coleman and Al Hail with me and he got a little peeved about it but he recorded it, because they were out of work and I put them back to work by doing that. So they wanted me in this particular place with a piano, bass, and drums - trio. So Klook and Oscar and all of them told me that they were barred out of Birdland. So I said come on and work with me. So with me when I went in this place I had Oscar Pettiford, Kenny Clarke on drums, Kenny Durham on trumpet, and Kai Winding on trombone. There was a terrific little thing happened. One night I felt that I wasn't accompanying the boys right so Bags - you know, with the Modern - came in and I said, "I have to go up to the ladies' rest-room. Will you sit and play a set for me?" He said, "Yes, Lou." So he sat down and while I was up there I was using toilet paper to write down the notes the way he was pushing. and When I came down it was much better. Because I had dropped
WILLIAMS

in from the East Side playing all that corn and with the cats. My whole thing is to needle the band to play their best for anybody who is soloing because if they play a good solo then I have inspiration to play.
But you just can't shift from the East Side -

Well, you can, but you can't shift overnight; you have to rehearse with them. We went in there and started blowing. Oscar was great to play with because we composed at least 3 tunes a night or more. He'd start a bass figure and I would play, and that is really my schtick, my whole way of doing. I like to compose while I'm playing. We had a great session going except then he was crazy about his "Moscow Mule". He'd go around the corner on Eighth Avenue and I'd have to go to get him. So one night I got a stick and I hit him on his knee and I said, "Listen, you had too much Moscow Mule." He laughed about it, you know, and I decided to put him on cello. So I called in Percy Heath, for bass, a terrific bass player also. So one night I was blowing like mad. Oscar was on the cello, he turned around and said, "You don't blow like that with me." I said, "Yes, because you high off of Moscow Mule." So I did put the musicians back to work there in this particular club. Charlie Parker came in one night and he said to me, "Lou, let's get a band or something together. You know all the cats always want me to get a band with you."
WILLIAMS 120

I said, "No, man, not the condition you're in." He said, "I'll do it, Mary. Anything you tell me I'll do." He said, "You know I'm not allowed to play in Birdland or any of the clubs." You know, that's during that period. So I told him, "Get up on the stand and let the people see how great you are." The place was really packed because see a lot of the people had followed me from the East Side. Some of these people had been to a ballet or something this night and they came in. They were all up in the balcony; it was Sunday night. Charlie Parker got up on the stand... he said, "Play the Kansas City Blues." Listen, I've never heard Coltrane play what that boy did! No! I talk about it often. When he finished the people in the place stood up and applauded. During the time that he played I don't know what carried us along with him because there were sounds that we'd never played before, Oscar and the bass and piano. To start out a blues - I think one of the guys had played one chorus...Charlie Parker kept going to keys and he kept going through changes... The one on the bass said, "Mary, where is he now?" I said, "Man, don't talk to me now," because Oscar said if anybody came up on the stand they were going to help him, so when Charlie stepped up there he said, "Lou, let's blow." So we were listening to his changes during it. I've never heard him play like that before in my life, the way he played.
WILLIAMS 121
When he finished everybody just screamed. He said, "How was that?" I said, "Man, that was too great for me."
But you still didn't go with him, in the band?
I didn't see him any more after that because later on I went to Europe. This was in the year of '52.
Was this when you worked with Woody Herman?

Ok yes. You know what really happened when I was on this engagement. My brother always comes around. He could really play drums but he never worked at it, piano - Jerry Burley, my brother. He's a dancer. He used to tap dance like Baby Laurence, the greatest dancer in the world, just never worked at anything like that. He happened to be in the club one night when I went in. No, it was later. I went to work one night and Glaser's always had an idea to put me with the Woody Herman group. I walked in and he didn't even tell me that he had fired all of my guys and had this band up here. I'm the only black person working in it. Well, that didn't bother me at all, but the idea that they didn't ask me if I wanted it. So Chick was standing against the wall and I said, "What happened, man?" He said, "They fired us." I said, "Like that, without a notice?" "Yes." He said, "You're going to be sorry because they ain't no other drummer you can play with." I said, "Oh, man, I don't want to hear that." But he told the truth because I haven't been able to play with anybody since
WILLIAMS

except Mickey Roker. I said, "This can't happen." So you know what - I'm kind of headstrong. I'll go your way or anybody's way with you for a while and if that stubborn streak hit me then you're in trouble. I'm not going to do any more. So my brother came in about 4 nights later to hear the group play. I was so mad sitting up there on the stand. Cat would tell you to play some of the tunes that they played with Woody Herman. They were trying to play some of the wrong changes according to the record. So I said, "They're wrong. You've given me the wrong changes on them and you're playing the wrong changes," what I'd figured out with my ear. All that kind of thing was going. I really missed my other guys anyway. So I told Billy Taylor, "Billy, came over and play this set. I got to go up to the ladies' restroom." He came over and I came down with my coat and hat on. I think it was in the winter. I think it was because in December I went to Europe. My brother happened to be there. He said, "Where you going?" He said, "You know you work for gangsters and they're tough. They'll do something." I said, "Listen, as mad as I am I'll take your head off. You better leave me alone." And I walked out. I left them up there and I walked out. So they tried to beg me, we'll give you $50 more, we'll give you this and that - because they were having crowds from the East Side. They followed me there. And I never went back.
WILLIAMS 123

That's when I had the offer to go to Europe. Gale's office called. They wanted to break a ban of 30 years, that had existed with the two unions, the English union and the American one. I don't even know what happened. It seems some English musicians came over here and they wouldn't allow them off the beat to play.
Jack Hilton's band?
I don't know. I heard something, so I got ready to leave to go to England. I had turned down offers before and I decided to go.
That gets us over to - you discussed your going to England. We talked about your going to England before and we got you over to Paris..( )

During the period that I was on 52nd Street and 8th Avenue with Billy Taylor, the boppers then were Bud Powell, Max Roach, Charlie Parker, and Kenny Durham. Most of the cats made their little complaints about Birdland and what they were doing. One day Max Roach and Bud Powell ran up and said, "Lou, you should come down and see how they're treating us and what's happening." I said, "O.K., I'll come down," but I didn't tell them when I was coming down. So I went down there and I slipped in on Bud Powell. I didn't see Max. Bud Powell was really gone; he was out of his mind. Something happened - it wasn't his drinking or smoking or anything else. I think from my feelings and Bud being around
WILLIAMS

me I think he was over-sensitive, you know. He felt every-body, felt everything because he was so terrific in his music. Usually when he'd get into these things I'd take him home and make him take a hot bath and just put him in my front room and make him sleep. When he got up he'd play like mad and he'd go like mad. But if he had an engagement at Birdland or places like that, for about 3 days he was all right and the fourth day he was gone, he was out of sight, and nobody could do anything with him. At one time Birdland offered me $75 a week to take care of him and all that. I said no, I have to work myself. Then too you'd have to have a man around, with him. But this particular time I slipped in on Bud and he was so funny till everybody in the place was laughing. He'd sit there playing, Art Tatum..... Shearing Sherry...... and he'd sit there and he'd look at the audience like this and when he got up from the piano he went around to the cash register and just went "Bing!" (Gory?) and took out what he wanted. I think John Gara, you know, who was with Sarah Vaughan, he grabbed him and said, "Come back, Bud." So when they put him off the stand, when I saw him I said, "Oh, so you want me to come down and help you and talk for you, and look what you did tonight." He said, "Ah, Baby Doll," - he called me Baby Doll. I knew when he was going off because he was a good friend, musical friend and everything else, but when he was going out of his
WILLIAMS

mind, going to the other planet, he felt I was his girl friend. I couldn't even have a little baby around the house; he kicked at my little nephew. He let nobody come near me. I said to him, "All right, I'm going to tell Monk what you did." Then he'd straighten up. I don't care what he was doing, if I told him I was going to tell Monk, he'd straighten up.
Why did that have an effect on him?

I don't know, I don't know why. I don't know if he was afraid of Monk or he respected him so much. So that's how I controlled him, through telling him I was going to get in touch with Monk. One time I held him here in the house and my brother got angry with me. I said, "I'm going to cure you of every thing you're doing." I kept him in the house two days and wouldn't allow him out. My brother came and said, "You shouldn't do that, because anything could happen to you." I said, "Not with him; he won't even steal from me." A lot of times the guys that were jealous of the cats coming up said, "Mary, they'll steal. They'll do this and that 'cause they'll need it, you know, for their drinks and whatnot." I said, "Nobody'll steal from me." Then I started planting money around to see if they would, and they wouldn't. Bud needed 50¢ one day and he said, "Hey, Baby Doll, give me 50¢." I said, "I haven't got it." He said, "Yes, you have. You have two
WILLIAMS 126

dollars and a half on the kitchen table." They wouldn't take anything from me, no. Whatever they were doing they never allowed me to do it, because one time I said to them, "Give me some of that, that you're doing." I was kidding with him. "Oh, Baby Doll," he got on his knees, "don't you ever do that."
Who were some of the other musicians you took care of?
Practically all of them.
Charlie Parker?

Oh, yes. Charlie Parker would always call and ask me if I liked some things he had written and when he did the strings he asked me to come down to Birdland. He said, "I want you to tell me really what you think of it, Lou." I went down. Charlie was a wonderful guy. I was at Birdland one day - you know that bar was terrible.
Terrible in what sense?

As I understand it, nice people never go to a bar. Well, not everybody's good, you know what I mean, but I'm talking about the character's you'll find mostly at bars, nice places, than you will sitting at a table. My schtick was hanging out at the bar with the guys, the musicians. So that's where you'd find me. He came up protecting me from a girl that had taken my pocketbook and he got it back for me and then drove me home that night.
WILLIAMS 127
He was a very nice person.
When you went down to hear the strings - you started to tell me about that. What happened then?
It was so great. I told him how great they were and he thanked me... I understand he recorded them later.
Did you help him with the strings?

No indeed. The only person I helped, Miles happened to be with me one day and Milton Oreny, the composer - he had so many masters in music till he couldn't play or write. Some people study too much. Milton and I were just saying a combination of things and I mentioned about a tuba and I think that that thing, that sound that Miles got on a record, was an idea of me just thinking of instruments, and he called me back and thanked me.
Was this when Miles had that 9-piece group?
Yes, that beautiful sound. We were all just sitting here naming instruments that we'd like to do things with, you know. He thanked me.
How about- you saw quite a bit of Miles, didn't you, during that period?

Oh, sure. We used to go to Birdland. It's the most peculiar thing to see him like he is now. I can't understand it. We'd be at Birdland and Miles had made some changes on Yesterday's. He'd say, "Look at this, Lou." You know, I'm a much better reader looking at music than I
WILLIAMS 128

am when I read it there, 'cause my mind starts wandering and I listen to the musicians and all that. It's a little confusing. He had brought in some changes on 'Yesterday.' I looked up at the stand and I looked at them. All of a sudden Fats Navarro, Charlie Parker, and all of them were so high until they had gone asleep. He said, "Look, look, Lou. I'd rather be something he is than to be in that condition." I understand a little later than that, maybe less than a year, Miles ran into Fats Navarro and Fats Navarro was out. Miles was so disgusted he said, "Man, give me that," and he went out with him. So that was the beginning of his drinking and whatnot. But he's a beautiful cat.
Do you see Miles at all these days?

No, but I like Miles. When I began praying Miles called me Reverend Williams and I gave him prayers and I sent him a lot of things. I played a concert with him in Europe about 3 years ago and he was all love and kisses and whatnot. I think he's very fond of me. I don't know what happened; I really don't know if all these things are as bad as some people say, but I think he became discouraged. I wasn't there but I heard during that period that I used to see him in Birdland, that Miles was abused by a policeman or something and he's been through several things like that. That can discourage one, you know what I mean, because if a man's outside catching the air and
WILLIAMS 129

trying to rest or do something like that and someone come up and abuse them for no reason whatsoever, well - I think a series of things like that happened to him to discourage him. I really don't know if he's as bad as what I hear, because I still like him and my brother Jerry is really crazy about him. I've had people to tell me to go down and see him. I said, "I don't want to go down and see him if he's in a bad way. He may not remember me as a person that he liked."
How was Max Roach in those days at Birdland that you're talking about? He had a period in which he was very upset and disturbed.

Yes, we were talking about that in Kansas City the other day. Something happened to him to change him around and he was very disturbed and upset and used to get in a lot of things. Now he's a very nice guy. I used to talk to Max Roach and Bud Powell about certain things. See, Max doesn't understand about a cross or anything. Max perhaps thinks that everything should come easy after a certain period. What I talked to them about, certain crosses you carry till you die. Things can't be smooth all the time. The only time I have a discussion, the way he thinks politically his political scene I never went for and I tell him.
What's his political - ?
WILLIAMS 130
His idea about life in that direction, I don't particularly go for it, you know.
Which direction is he looking at?
Nonsense to me. It wasn't going to make it. I saw him over at the UN once and we got in a discussion. I said, 'Wait a minute, now stop, let me tell you something, bla-bla,' and I give it to him.
What's he advocating?

Well, the mistreatment of the black man, but after a while as far as I'm concerned, that's just a detraction to my music. I should stick to my music and maybe someday that will disappear, because I feel my music is like a prayer.
Have you ever been interested in politics at all?

Yes, I got hung up in it through working in the Cafe, but I think all musicians or people like me would get mixed up in something, looking for some people to help them and help the race. But they can never be anything but a musician. Through doing benefits and a lot of other things, and you don't know how serious it is - but there's not one musician I think would be in any kind of political anything if they weren't disturbed about the race, as being abused and whatnot of the race, trying to help the poor. I've been in practically everything but I've come out of it. It doesn't take me a year to find out that it's wrong.
WILLIAMS 131
Do you find most of them, most of the things you have been interested in, were wrong?

Yes, I found out and discovered that in the end the best thing for me to do is stick with my music. If I believe in a political thing or something like that, I push other people. Believe it or not, I've never voted, but I think I can get more votes than anybody else. If I think there's a good man out there, if I have time to think about it, I usually try to get people to vote for him. Well, I'll tell you what happened in Kansas City. We were living there and Johnny Harrington and I, a clarinet player, he and his wife went downtown and voted. I don't think anybody else. Maybe Andy did or some of the boys thought about it or remembered to vote. About 3 months after the election they were charging him tax on somebody else's furniture. They found out where he was.
It's dangerous.
So I never voted after that.
Have you ever gotten interested at all in the idea of Africa as a home for blacks?

Never. I learned about Africa when I was 12, during that period. I learned all about the whole history of Africa because my great-grandparents used to talk about that, about Africans, how they were brought over. I think I probably know the whole scene on it - how they were sold
WILLIAMS

by the chiefs and all that. I would never be interested in Africa. I believe that I wouldn't be able to live in Africa because of their ways. I have quite a few friends from Africa and they just think different than I do, well me want to being a musician naturally. I wouldn't/Be over there nor would I want to see Americans go back because - what they don't understand there are so many black people, Americans, they put them in concentration camps because Africans and Indians Westerners are jealous of Americans. They think they're rich and they're a rich country. They're jealous of the jazz, the spiritual, that was created and made such a big hit at one time. I read articles in Europe when I went there that they don't want us there. They just want people that can help teach their kids or to help them. Whenever a black American buys property, he buys a house and not the land. A lot of things, they don't want them living there, except artists or somebody that can help them. I've had dealings with them to know that they're dangerous and the worst thing that could happen was the black magic that the black Americans went into because it's so strong it could destroy. They don't know how to deal with anything like that, especially musicians that are playing that type of music. They've got to bedestroyed in the end, because that's not our way of living and how we've been brought up. We've been brought up as Americans. What /We should do is
WILLIAMS

get something going in a love way to fight conditions here and get rid of conditions and be our freedom here, because if we have to go to another country to help us to be freed in America, we all should go somewhere away from here, because it's not going to happen that way. I never wanted to go even to Europe. I like America. If everybody was like me, all the money wouldn't be over there, 'cause when I make some I bring it back. I don't spend any of it, 'cause you can find everything they have over here. Because when you do go to Europe and talk with people, they're all jealous because they think we have the money. This is a young country. One day we're not going to have anything because we're so gullible over there. Africa really laid a bomb on the black Americans. That was one of the sweetest races and one of the purest races. I said to Peter and he laughed at me, "The Germans thought their race was pure. Suffering makes you pure. Who's got the purest race if you was going to go there and talk about nonsense like that? It would be the black man." At one time they were the sweetest. Now it is Uncle Tom-ish to see a man out on the street dancing and he has a dime in his pocket, but if you look at it in another way, that man was happy. If you look at it and say, how in the world could somebody do that and he has no money and don't know where he's going to eat. At one time they were just that happy. Somebody had
WILLIAMS 134

to disturb them so until they're out of their mind. You can't even tell them when they're going wrong and what they're doing and they've got 'em knocking the white man and yet they're still afraid of him. I think... those people like that, like the Jehovah's Witnesses, now, I'm not talking about religion and all that - they know when to strike, when to try to get you in. That's the reason why I went through all the religions, practically all of them, Muslims and everything, threw books out the window and asked God to keep me around the corner to the Catholic church. That's my way.
When did you start going through all the religions? When did that happen?
During the period when most of the musicians were becoming Muslims.
Was that after the World War, during the World War?
This was before I went to Europe.
Late 1940's?

They'd bring the books up here and anything I don't understand and if the words aren't in the dictionary or some kind of language, I don't bother with it. I don't bother with it. I think I can understand practically everything. If I was reading French and couldn't understand the words I'd get the dictionary. But I don't understand what
WILLIAMS 135

their thoughts were. The Muslims, as I understand it, later on it's the devil, because the religion is really the Moslems. I just heard that; I don't know; I haven't gone into it deeply. It's apolitical thing that they introduced to America. Everything that comes from Europe and is introduced in America becomes an evil and I don't understand it. These other things in Europe - there's a lot of love among the Muslims, Moslems - there's a lot of love. I told some people: "Black people love white people and vice versa." So the last time I was there when I played the concert with Miles Davis. I saw this girl, she sneaked on the bus and she had a white baby in her arms, this black girl. She was a Muslim in America and she had a white husband. Now she divorced her husband and he divorced her. He married a white girl and she married a white man. I looked at her. She was trying to hide from me because before she was talking against white people. I looked at her and I said, "I told you!" That's all I said to her. She said, "Yes, Mary, I understand what you meant." I said when anything is introduced in America it becomes an evil. There's hatred in it and I don't know why.
How did you arrive at what you found was the right thing to do?
Well, because there was so much confusion in everything else and I couldn't understand it. I read the
WILLIAMS

Jehovah's Witness things. When I was reading a little pamphlet I found out that there was a man - I don't know if this is true or not - one man receives all the money and he has everybody out on the street working for him. I think God is a little different than that. You work together and you share. Now if you're head of an organization or something you have to have money in escrow or save money to save it and pay for things and help the poor. Their only concern is pulling people in off the street and through my experience, you can become a fanatic when you deal with God. If I grab you and started pulling you into a religion, which I did, the reason I can tell you this - I'm a guinea pig. I can become a fanatic because when you start dealing with God you have to be very careful. Once that comes about, I'm telling you that's the end of it. You have to take it easy with people if you're going to win them over for God. You can't just be sticking material in the door and pulling them and talking and all that kind of stuff. You pray for them and you do it the easy way. Now I did that and Father Woods said to me, "You want to go to a psychiatrist? I'm going to send you to one." They remind me of fanatics.
How did you get into this whole thing, Mary?
We left you over in Paris...
What I really, how I got into it, I left America
WILLIAMS

and of course you know I went to Europe when the ban was broken there. How I broke the ban was that I played with all the musicians in Europe, all the bands and all the musicians in England, London, and all over. I happened to be at a party that Lascelles, you know, he's the Queen's cousin, he gave a party for Garland Wilson and I. There happened to be a little GI there, black soldier. He said, "You look disturbed, upset." I said, "Yeah, I'm trying to get out of England." The newspapers and the people were if you beautiful but you see/were born in New York, a fast-thinking country, you're held back. Like the guy with the newspaper that says, "Why is it that Americans come over here and after a while they're going so fast until they meet themselves going and coming. Everybody's looking at them." It happens like that. I was held over. I was supposed to go there for 9 days or 11 days and I was held over 11 months. The newspaper did this. So at this party I was just anxious. I wanted to get out. He says, "My grandmother always told me to read the 91st Psalm." Well, you know I never could drink and I had had about 3 Scotches. I was drunk. So I misunderstood him; I thought he said read all the Psalms. It took me two days; however, it worked. Everybody was so nice like the S. S. United cooks and all the guys on the S. S. United. They knew that the food wasn't good and they used to bring me like 50 steaks. They were the most delicious steaks. They'd bring them to the house and I'd give them to
WILLIAMS

people, you know what I mean, because there were too many, they'd spoil. They knew I was going to have a birthday party and so the cook on the ship baked me a birthday cake. The guys were coming to enjoy themselves and I had the room and everything. All of a sudden I left the room open and locked all my bags and left them there and went to Paris, just like that. When they came they called all over Paris and everything. I went over there with Nicole Barclay, who owned the Blue Star Records, I think. I went to visit her. I never went back. So they had a party. I don't know what happened but -
One thing I don't understand. Reading all the Psalms, what did that do to you?

You know what that did? I discovered I was stuck and it uprooted me like it would a tree when a storm hit it and moved me on to things I was supposed to be doing. I wasn't supposed to be there because the last two months I hadn't worked at all. I was finished in England until a later date. You know, you can stay too long. In Europe if you go there, when you go in fresh you get maybe $100 a night but if you keep staying it gets smaller and smaller. I just couldn't get away.
How did reading the Psalms unstick you?
Have you ever read the Psalms? Any of them?
Sure -
You're calling for help madly.
WILLIAMS 139
But I never read all of them.
Well, that's what I did.
What effect did it have on you. Did it make you get up and move, was that the idea?

You're crying out so for God's help till you shed everything, everything that's holding you back. You see, sometimes we can get hung up in a situation and can't get out. You know, it's just like a magnet; it keeps holding you. Sometimes we can get out too soon. We don't let it worry us but some things can just drag and drag and drag. You feel, I'm finished here. Like, I've been in a night club. They'd want to held me over and I'd say no, I'm gone. Because until a later date, because you peter out, see, completely. So that's what I felt. But what this does - you have to do it to find out. But it's magic.
When you got to Paris what happened?

All during my lifetime I made more money than I've ever made in my life. I was working in Bœuf sur le Toit. My best friend, Garland Wilson, great pianist, he knew he wasn't going to live long and he always loved me from the first day he met me and I loved him. He came to England. He said, "I came here because I heard you were here. The doctors give me 6 months to live and I'm going to die with you, where you are." I said, "I'm going so fast I don't know if you can keep up if you're sick."
WILLIAMS 140

He said, 'I'm not kidding.' I said, 'Oh, go on with you. You look so fat and healthy.' So when I left England he was right in back of me. So we had a suite of rooms together and Garland used to come and he'd just lay across the foot of my bed all night. we'd sleep like that. I was picking up his sickness. I was getting sick and he was getting well. The Baroness Koenigswarter came and brought me medicine and whatnot. She thought I had a cold but it was Garland. I had to sleep away from him. Shortly after that he passed away.
What did he have?
Complications of something, I don't know. He had told me but I forgot.
Did you actually pick it up from him?

Yes, I was. He was getting stronger and I was getting weak, just going down, down, down. So he was working in the Boeuf sur le Toit and certain people they didn't allow to work in there, especially a woman. Not didn't allow but they just didn't go for women as much as they did men. So what I did was to take over his job and they loved me because they loved Garland, not because I was Mary but because they loved him. So I worked in there and I made good money and I doubled at the theatre. All the Americans had camp back to America and the theatre had to pay what I asked for. It was so successful with an American
WILLIAMS 141

musician there so they wanted me in. I doubled from the theatre back to the night club. So all of a sudden I just walked off from both gigs. It was a good thing that I knew Gerard Pochonet, a French drummer that played with all the Americans there, because he took me out to his grandmother's house in the country.
Stop here while we change tapes.
You went with Gerard Pochonet to the country to live with his grandmother?

Yes, I went to live with his grandmother. Gerard was a wonderful guy. Gerard was the type of drummer who played for most of the Americans, like Lena Horne, Hazel Scott, and all the great stars when they came in. He had such a terrific beat on drums, and feeling. He was a newspaper man; he was an all-around man and one good thing about him, when musicians were stranded or needed help or recording dates, he always helped them, especially the Americans. He favored them because he just loved their music. So he took me out in the country and I stayed there with him, I guess about 6, 7, or 8 months before coming back to America. I canceled everything. I wouldn't go out with anybody to work or anything. All I did was pray and eat and sleep.
What got you started praying?
The incident in England when the guy told me to
WILLIAMS 142
read the 91st Psalm.
Had you prayed ever since then?

Yes, I never stopped even up until now. You know really, John, what I think happened to me, I was going to tell you - I have been a very psychic person. I was born a psychic person. You know in the beginning of the story I told you, but what I did, I put that in my music. Like I told you once before that I could, if I was playing with any musician on earth - it could be Charlie Parker - I could almost hear, could hear most of the time, the next note they're going to play. All this was in my music to help me musically, because I've done some fantastic things, you know, and not studied as much as other musicians in the music field. So I think what happened to me after I stopped playing then my vision and everything went on the outside of music and I began to hear what was going to happen musically while I was praying. Like I saw Charlie Parker's death. I felt that a strange foreign sound would enter into the strains of jazz and would destroy the heritage, would destroy jazz completely. Jazz came out of the spirituals; ragtime, Kansas City swing - well, the 1929 year of jazz bands, Kansas City swing, boogie and the blues of that era. Well, the blues has always been there, that's a spiritual feeling. The next era was bop. Now we've waited I don't know how many
WILLIAMS 143

years for a new sound in jazz and it hasn't come forth as yet. I could see all this happening while I was in Paris. It kind of frightened me. It seemed like my feelings was altogether out on the street, or what was happening in the world. I was able to make several predictions maybe 20 years ahead. Some of the predictions that I had was, are black musicians losing our rich heritage, called jazz. The only bad thing about it is the name jazz and I think all the musicians in all eras of jazz have tried to change that name. My era was the swing era and we tried to change it. Also I saw Charlie Parker's death and also very, very bad disturbance among black people, as far as the riots. They've been so disturbed until they're going in the wrong direction and losing the beauty that they had gained through suffering.

We're talking about basically a period when you were in France and you had gone out to Gerard Pochonet's grandmother's and were staying there. How did this affect you then? What followed the time that you were out at his grandmother's?

I wanted to come home very fast and see what help I could be, you know especially with Charlie Parker. When I did arrive my brother happened to see him coming out of the hospital with sneakers on. My brother Jerry called me from Harlem Hospital and said, 'Mary, I just saw Charlie

and it's below zero. Have you got any money or anything you can do to help him?" I said, well, tell him to come by the house. He had Charlie to talk with me and Charlie promised to come up the next day or so. That's the day that he was on the way to the Baroness. He went to her place instead. I thought maybe if I came home there was something I could do about talking or doing something with the musicians or helping.
When you got back there, what happened? Had you planned to go on playing?

I don't know what I had in mind. My only thoughts were of helping my people, because I saw all these terrible things, like you would looking at TV. I saw these things happening and all these terrible riots and whatnot. Gerard used to say in Paris, he said I was crazy, but he learned later on after he came to America that I wasn't. Thank God for Father Woods because Father Woods got me out of it completely and back to music.
Who was Father Woods?
Father Woods was my confessor. Professor Barry Ulanov got a hold of him to give me instructions.
We'll go back further. You came back to the United States from France. Were you going to church then or...
I went to church a couple of times there with
WILLIAMS 145
a couple of friends. But I really started going to church when I came back to America.
Tell me about, just before we get into that, what was your religious background as a child, for example?

It wasn't too much because I came out of the church. I was Baptist then. Most of my sisters and brothers were baptized Catholic and I saw so many things going down with the preacher and what was happening in the church, I felt that I shouldn't even be there. So I came out; I never went to church any more. As I said before this, I didn't know if I did in the first part of my story, I met an insurance man who used to follow me when I was with the Andy Kirk band. I was at the Apollo Theatre. He'd get a cab and hold the cab all during the time the show was on, all day. He was a very, very wealthy man. He'd come back stage and he'd have gifts for me. One thing that he gave me was a little white Bible and he told me, 'This is your wealth and your health and always keep it.' Well, I kept this Bible with me but I never read it. So what happened, I never even thought about praying or doing anything until after Europe in the 50's and I got a sound, that everybody should pray in the church every day because the world would change and you would encounter selfish people and a lot of selfishness in the world. So the only church I followed was the Catholic church and I used to go in and meditate and pray.
WILLIAMS 146
Did you try other churches first?

Yes, other religions. When I returned I went to several religions. I was working with a dancer who became a preacher at 125th Street and Seventh Avenue in a church there. He was snatching people off the street baptizing. You know what really happened during that period? A lot of musicians and dancers became preachers and they began to preach. They must have gotten the same thing. This dancer I worked with until I began - I think I got together the Bel Canto Foundation to help dope addicts and alcoholics, musicians.
With this dancer or by yourself?
No, no, no, by myself. I left him after I began praying in the Catholic church.
But then you finally decided on the Catholic church because it was open, was that the reason?
Yes, that was the only reason. Well, the other reason is that was the only church that I felt good in, that I could meditate without vibes hitting me in the head.
Was this the period when you just went to the church every day and prayed?
Yes, I prayed. I prayed for everybody but myself until Father Crowley says, 'Listen, you better pray for yourself too while you're praying for everybody.'
WILLIAMS 147
Who's Father Crowley?

Father Crowley, he was concerned about, after he heard I had stopped playing, he was traveling around with the Newport Jazz Festival and Father O'Connor. They both were friends. So he began coming around to try to get me out to play. He came to the house and he told Dizzy and Elaine, "Mary is a saint." They said, "Why would you say this?" He said, "You should go to her house." I had people in here from the Welfare and everywhere and I was sleeping on the floor. I was feeding and clothing them and doing a lot of things with them, you know.
Now you weren't working at this point?
No, I wasn't working.
Where did you get the money to feed and clothe them?

I had royalties coming in and friends helped, especially Dizzy Gillespie and Lorraine. I never asked them for anything in my life, but it seems like they were in tune with me. Days I thought I wouldn't have anything to eat - Dizzy's cousin (or a nephew), his name is Boo Frazier - he'd ring the doorbell and he'd have a basket full of food for me - hams, steaks, and a lot of things in there. Lorraine said, "I thought you were hungry so I sent you some food." They were really beautiful; they looked after me and they were so kind to me.
WILLIAMS 148
Had you met Father Woods before Father Crowley?

No, you see, what I was going to tell you, that Father Crowley told Barry what I was doing. He took me down to Barry Ulanov's house. He spoke to him about me, the things that I was doing. He said, "She should be Catholic. Get a priest for her. She wants to be Catholic." So Barry said, "I'll get one of the greatest priest's that's ever lived." He got hold of Father Woods and he was really something else. Dizzy loved him and all the musicians.
What is Father Woods' first name?

Father Anthony Woods, S. J., Jesuit. I'm telling you he was something else. When he passed away about 6 or 8 years ago I thought I was going to die myself. I didn't know I was leaning so hard. He did everything in his power to help me back to music and things that were still happening with me in a strange way, all this ESP working. He told me to call him any time and sometimes I called him 4 o'clock in the morning. He and Lorraine Gillespie, they had a ball on the phone when they talked about me. It was so funny, some of the things I'd call them about. He was so very kind to me. He went along with me and he finally got me back to jazz. When I went in the Hickory House about 7 years ago, he was there practically every night.
WILLIAMS 149
Why did you stop playing?

Well, I didn't really stop on my own. Something carried me away; I began praying and I never thought about playing any more. I just thought about helping people other than - as I understand and have experienced that God was helping many souls through music, but I decided to help them in flesh instead of playing for them. I understand that you can offer it up every note you play to help some /souls and things like that but I was going on my own without the talent. The talent was much stronger for helping people.
How did Father Crowley convince you to go back to playing?

Father Crowley and Father O'Connor talked to me, several priests. They also asked me to write a Mass, but Father Woods is the only one that really stuck with me until I really began praying, and Dizzy. Dizzy would send Melba, "Go up there and see what Lou's doing. See how she's playing." Melba, I understand, would go back and say, "Man, Lou played some chords and you ought to hear them. They're really great." He said, "Well, get her out." Melba would come here and when he took me out to the Newport Jazz Festival, Melba arranged some things. He said, "Those arrangements were really good." She said, "I didn't do them. That was Lou's arrangement. I was in the room and I just sat
WILLIAMS 150

down and took the music down." He said, "What! Get her out here!" He finally got me out to Newport where they were all wheeling like mad, like most of the priests did, to get me to write a Mass. Father O'Connor said, "Well, I tell you, if you don't write a Mass just play it, play it on the piano, Mass." Oh, just terrible. My first experience in getting back into the atmosphere was just awful. See, I had stayed in the house away from people so long and after I did the Newport Festival the next thing was - let's see, what's the name of that club, piano house on 56th and -
It's not there any more. I know, begins with a C.

The name of that room was the Composer Room. That was the most beautiful room and I loved it. But the craziest thing happened. We had two managers there and the crowds were tremendous. Even Miles Davis called and said, 'Why don't you come out and record with me?' They were working like mad to get me to come out and play. Well, I was going to tell you what happened in the Composer Room. I hadn't been around people in a long time. When I came off the stand I'd run to the checkroom and hide behind the coats. People like Pops Whitaker from the New Yorker, Robert Sylvester, and a lot of newspaper men. At one time I used to pal around with them. I'd go to the News or something for dinner and all that. I think they thought I was a little bit wacky too. I'd get off the stand and run to the checkroom, so the checkroom girl called the owner and said, 'Listen, I can't hang up the clothes for that trio that you booked here! So she runs to the checkroom and two musicians are doing the same thing.' The bass player
WILLIAMS 152

and the drummer, Bill Clark and my bass player, they were running to the checkroom with me after a while. I guess they thought something bad was going to happen and I was trying to get to the checkroom. I did this for about 3 weeks and after a while Sy, Sy Baron, that was his name (he's a lovely cat) said to me, "Mary, you're going to have to come out of that checkroom." "I'm not, I'm not." So he finally coaxed me out and I sat with the people. I'd sit in the corner as if I was having a chill. It's just terrible to get away from people 6 months or a year and then go around them. When you say he was with you there what do you mean?
He used to go down and sit with me, see that I didn't walk out the door. I was upset, nervous I guess.
You mentioned the fact that people were asking you to write a mass. Had you started working on that at this particular time?

No, I wanted to write one but I didn't know just the type of music until St. Martin de Porres was canonized in '62 and I wrote this thing, St. Martin de Porres, dedicated to him. I tried to get a lyricist and all but I took the
WILLIAMS 153

lyric to Father Woods and he said, no, they didn't capture the spirit of St. Martin. So I told him, "Well, you do it." He said, "I never wrote anything in poetry in my life, Mary, and can't do it." I said, "I'll tap it out for you." I did and he wrote a very beautiful lyric, he did, he wrote it. He had never written one before. So I asked him, "Let's do a blues." He said, "O.K." I said, "I'll get some slang words from Babs Gonzales." He said, "O.K." I said, "I'll call you tomorrow night." When I called back with all this slang I said "coat"; he said "rug"; "car"; he said "short" "chorus". He knew all the words. That's how he was, you see.

But getting back to Babs Gonzales, you know I haven't told you something about this terrific character that's so fantastic. He wrote some of the greatest books on the slang idiom. He said, "Listen Mary, I've written a book." He took this book to a disc jockey... This guy used his entire book and had it published under his name, Fred Robinson. So Babs said, "Oh, that's all right," and he used to dance around. The next thing musicians were recording his compositions and what-not and he became so bitter about it till he began to go
WILLIAMS

around town fighting. I used to meet him and he'd say, "Lou, I'm really sick of what they're doing to me." He was so talented; he could create all these various things that he sang. One time he went down to the Roost - or Broadway I think it was the Roost, Rooster or something like that - and Erroll Garner was playing and he started some stuff there. They said Babs used to carry red pepper in his hands. He was under a fan and he was trying to throw this in the manager's eyes and the fan blew it back in his eyes. He was going all around town just in a bad way. So I said, "Babs, if I were you I wouldn't do that." He said "What let people take advantage of you and steal all your material and that everything?" And from that day on was the nicest guy that I've ever seen in my life. He used to get jobs for anybody that was out of work and do the craziest and nicest things for them and all of a sudden he changed, losing so much. One day I got kind of angry because somebody owed me some royalties and he met me downtown. I was puffing and blowing... and I was so mad. He said, "Oh, so you're the lady that told me to stop fighting!" But I've seen some of the material he's written and it's so different and so great. I've just heard here recently, and I've just said to myself, I'll be glad when he gets back the way he used to be.
WILLIAMS 155

He said he thought I was coming because I thought maybe he was going to die, so he went and got this wine and drank it. But I used to have a ball. I'd go to the mass in the morning, 7 o'clock mass, and sat through all the masses. I'd get out about 9 or 10. I'd come home and fix lunch for all the poor people I had in the house I was feeding. I'd go right back and meditate a couple hours and then I'd come home. I was from the house to the store to the church.
That was your life then? When did you start the Bel Canto Foundation?
I don't know what year it was but it was during that period while I was praying.
How did it start?

I decided that I wanted to help the few - well, after comparing rock I said the few - few musicians that were using dope, jazz musicians that were using dope. I decided I'd like to help them and so I went on out on my own with a method of my own. I had success with two.
What was your method?
Prayers and music, either give them Psalms to
WILLIAMS

read or write something. Like I had a drummer that was on it and his wife timed him. It took him 5 minutes to go home. He'd come here 8 o'clock in the morning and I'd just keep him in the house. One time I took him to the Five and Ten and I forgot to give him breakfast. I said, oh, I hope he doesn't steal anything while we're in here. Sure enough, he told me this two or three years later. I said, "Man, I was praying for you that you didn't steal anything." ... This guy, it must have been in his mind or something because he was cured so very fast, but later on I had to take him to someone for injections and whatnot to counteract what he was doing. The first night I had him here in the house he began to want a fix and so I said, "I just wrote a drum part." I wrote and I wrote and I said, "Dig this." He said, "Yeah." I said, "Well, play it." He had a pad, and ... He played it and he forgot. Everytime that happened I said, "Hey," and I'd write something else. That worked on him I noticed that night because it took his mind off completely... or else the staff. They gave him was so weak.
WILLIAMS

night he didn't have anything from 8 o'clock till 12 o'clock at night. I usually sent him home around 11 or 12 and I'd call his wife and say, "Five minutes is up. Is he there?" She'd say yes. So that's how I did that.

The other person was a dealer but they told me what they were and I kept them. Father Crowley said to me, "Listen, what you're doing is very dangerous." I said, "I don't care as long as I'm helping them, a poor person." This other one he got away from it completely.
What was the Bel Canto Foundation?
It was a foundation to help dope addicts and alcoholics.

very wealthy people and if I got them I couldn't move them in the store. One girl, one of the cousins of the Mellons, was here - Peggy Hitchcock, she was very good to me. She gave me her trousseau. WILLIAMS 161
priest, called me from California. He used to call me practically every week to find out what I was doing.
Where did you first meet him - the Hickory House? Where did you first meet Father O'Brien?

in Harlem. I was trying to bring white patrons back to Harlem. A lot of them did come up while I was there. money for 4 weeks to pay my rent, electric light, and everything and I sat down there and played and Peter run around. So that was the beginning of our thing and we went through/and he borrowed a lot of strain money and he did a lot of things, from his parents and what-not. He's a real good friend to have.

Two years ago.

Dizzy would book me - not book me but he'd recommend me for various places. I don't guess I had over 3 or 4 jobs a year. But the strangest thing happened. I existed enough to help others.
