I spoke to her and asked her and she came back to me in a dream and said to me
WILLIAMS

that they chained her down like that in a house. Well, they did. People took her house from her and just had her in a bed and she wasn't being fed and a lot of things. Levy, the owner, one of the brothers of Birdland got killed and I called Father Woods and I said to him, "There's a man here from Birdland - " - I used to call him Father - the silliest thing - that's what he and Lorraine used to laugh about over the phone - and I picked up the News, somebody came to the house or something and brought the News in and Levy, they read where he'd gotten killed. He'd come to the house for a prayer. People like that, after a while I was so polluted with friends or things dying or getting killed that I began to go to church and get those brown candles for the dead. I became frightened here in the house, you know, and I'd get brown candles and burn them for the dead in the house. After a while I got rid of that completely, after I became Catholic. This was during the period when I was taking my instructions. Strange things like that were happening to me.

There was another guy, a newspaper man. I can't remember his name, with King Features. He was a very good friend of mine. He used to come and take me out and Peter (ran up?) Rabbit - well, this hasn't been too long ago and he was telling me about his death or something. I said, "He was
WILLIAMS 174
here last night; he came to me in a dream." Even if that happens to me now and somebody dies, I'll go and have a Novena done on them. All that opened up since I was praying.
Once you got back into music and were not praying as constantly as you had been, was there a change in anything?

Yes, there was a little change because you see, what I was trying to tell you, that ESP was in my music and the more music I played and the more jobs, it's not so much now, just a little. Maybe once or twice a year or three times a year. See, it's getting back into the music again, but it was on the outside. That's the reason why I told you that story so you'd know what had happened. See I had very good - I was better than Dixon, that woman in Washington, but I didn't know it; see, it was in my music.
Somehow it's going back in.

It's going back in. I'm seeing less and less of these things but if anything important - I had a flash about 2 or 3 months ago. I've forgotten what it was. A strange thing used to happen to me too, say for instance I've never been to your house and all of a sudden maybe one day I could see you walking into your house, or I could see you. You know? That used to happen, things like that. They were just terrible for a while. I could hear people talking about me. Lorraine and Dizzy were saying something one day - this was before I began really playing.
WILLIAMS

They were saying one day, "Has she given it to you/yet?" I was coming down the hall and I heard Lorraine say, "No." He said, "Well, I gave her some bla-bla..." I had a pocketbook that Hazel had brought back from Paris and it was worth, oh, $300, a beaded pocketbook. She gave it to me to raise money, Hazel Scott. Lorraine liked it but I didn't know whether I should give it - I wanted to give it to Lorraine. So that night I called Father and I said - and Father said, "Yes, they're your friends, Mary." Lorraine called me and she said, "Guess what? I was just talking to Dizzy about you. Dizzy asked if you still had the pocketbook. I said Mary's not going to give that pocketbook; Mary's honest and she knows she has to raise money with it and I don't have the money to buy it." So what I finally did, I returned it to Hazel because I couldn't - it was new, a beautiful pocketbook and I couldn't raise money.
and the Jazz Festival.
Tell me about Cardinal Wright in Pittsburgh.

Yes, that is something else. Father Woods got in touch with him. See, I went to Pittsburgh, I was back and forth to Pittsburgh for two years. Father called me one day and said, "Why don't you come back to New York to play your music. I'll tell you what to do. Get in touch with (he was a Bishop then) Bishop Wright." He wired Bishop Wright; A friend of mine, A.W. Stubble, wired him.
WILLIAMS 176

And so Father Woods had gotten in touch with me to help me. He saw me right away. So I had never been in front of a Bishop and I felt so strange. I just looked at him, you know, with all these colors on and everything. He said, "What can I do for you?" I said, "Jazz, jazz. There won't be any jazz after while." He looked at me and I told him about mother. He had confirmed them and all these people and he loved her, because he has - he does many, many favors for black people. He cleaned up Wiley Avenue where the dope addicts and all that was and he just does a lot of favors. I understood that he gave a man $12,000 for a project and the Ku Klux burned a cross on him before he went to Europe because he did that, you know, it was publicized. So he threw up his hands and he said, "We'll put on a festival for you." He must have gotten somebody least to put up at 50 to 75 thousand dollars because the musicians cast tossed $25,000 dollars to go in. So they did this festival every year. I got out of it because I got hold of George Weir to do it and I didn't think I should go down as a producer of a thing like that. I just let him take it all over himself, you know. I did two or three of the concerts, then I got out of it because I didn't want to wear myself out in Pittsburgh.
What was wrong with Pittsburgh?
It was a pretty tough town. The reason I went
WILLIAMS
was because that is not an artistic town. Sometimes you can be lucky enough to start something up that's never happened in an old rusty broken-down town like that.
What's happened with the festival? Are they still going on with it?
... They failed in it so they got George Wein (Wing?) back over there again. The Gulf Oil was sponsoring one cat over there and it wasn't too good.
Then there was another period, wasn't there, Mary, in 1968 when you went to Copenhagen and Rome?
Oh, yes, that was wonderful. I went over to open a new club of Baron Timme Rosencranz, a real baron...
This was in Copenhagen?

Copenhagen, yes. Well, I asked her that I wanted to go. Things like that happened to me. I didn't know that he was sick and I just thought I was going over to help him. It was a nice engagement except that I didn't work for about 2 months. They were still building the club. It was a very nice engagement.
And then you went to Rome after that?

I went through Rome but I had been to Rome - yes, I think that's when we put on the first jazz mass but it didn't really go through. They had newspapers out from everywhere, from all other countries and everywhere else,
WILLIAMS 178

because there had never been a jazz mass in Rome. What they did, what really stopped it, the Italians like to be told what they're going to do but everybody was afraid to tell them because it would have taken them another year to say yes. So they said, well, let's do it fast. It would have gone through but the girl at the Vatican radio caught us or played it smart. She came in one afternoon while we were rehearsing and said, "Guess what, I just broadcast the mass right on the lap of the Pope." The Pope listened to the radio at certain times. Everybody said, "Oh, my goodness, oh, oh." And so they told the Cardinal not to do it. Yes, because they didn't like people coming to their country like that, doing things. So it was done as a concert after the mass.
As things are now, Mary, are you active in the church?
Yes, I'm very active but I don't go to church every day. I go Sundays or Saturday mass. I used to go every day.
Why have you cut down?

Most of the thing is going into my work now and I didn't have anything to do then when I was doing that. Then that is too much anyway to go every day. It's all right. It's good if you can do it but then there's a chance
WILLIAMS
of you not going at all through going every day, you get sick of it. What I was doing, when it was time I guess for me to cut out on it, it happened.
In other words, that period when you were going every day, you don't feel that you overdid it?

No, because I needed the strength. The world can destroy me - not really, I'm a strong woman through being around men, but I could really be bent badly, you know, being in the company of people and things like that. I think what it does is to put an aura around me and to strengthen me to do further work for God.
You mentioned being around men all the time. You spent your whole life really in a man's world.

On his lap and in his world, yet I'm feminine. You know, some women they change their sex after they've been around men like that all the time, but being around men gave me, you know, like Monk said once when he was here at the house and Nelly, his wife was talking to him. He says, "I won't listen to silly women. Mary's the only woman I'll take any advice from." See, they taught me their trend of thought and their way of thinking. I'd rather gossip in front of a man because it really isn't gossip. You're talking to have fun, you know, it's something to laugh about. But if I did that with a woman
WILLIAMS 180

it would be all over the country and it would be gossip, they just sound different. Now I feel I'm out of place... I know some very good women musicians but I'm just out of place with them. If I had to do a battle or anything with them I wouldn't play nothing because I do have something like this happen, that they're not my equal, and that's very bad. That could be prejudice or something's the matter. I never want to be prejudiced or something like that, but there's something else, John, something like they're still thinking this way and I don't think that way. I withdraw. If I had a contest or had to do something with another woman, she'd win; I'd give it to her because she doesn't matter to me that much. I never thought about breaking that because it isn't important. I don't harm anybody through it.
Except you wouldn't give it to them on piano, would you?

I'd let them have anything they want. It doesn't matter because they're not my equal in thinking. They can be most intelligent or anything else, I have something that has been embedded in me through good strong men, and men that were real good men and you don't find them today.
Did you have trouble being accepted as a musician by another women?
Never, that's the thing about it, that's the
WILLIAMS 181

reason why I don't understand - never in my life. When Earl Hines had his little band and was playing for afternoon things in Pittsburgh, the boys after the session would come and get me. It's always been that. They'd come and get me and take me to play and anything, if I was playing wrong, they showed me. I was just like one of the boys.
You have always worked with black music, right or not?
Well, what do you mean when you say that?
This is what you've been playing.
That's what I like but I haven't always done that. I learned the classics through the set player. I had to get my other 50¢ a week.
Would you have liked to have played classical music?

No, I don't think so. A concert pianist told me - Robert Harris been trying to get me to do that. He heard me when I was really in good form at the Hickory House. You know, the same reason I won't play commercial rock. Commercial rock makes you corny. Jazz pushes off, you know, like an eighth note tied/over to a quarter in the next bar. It pushes off, it goes easy, like this, but rock, 1-2-3-4-bop, like that... I don't want to get stiff like that. I had a drummer and a bass player to kind of stiffen me out a couple of times. I played with them a while and was kind
WILLIAMS 182

of happy I got away from them. But that's the reason why I'm afraid if I played the classics and went all the way with it I'd lose the feeling of the greatest (now I'm not putting the classics down) - the greatest music that I think has ever been -'cause I can write the classics and everything here. I can write that too you know, once I get into it. One day - my husband, he was kind of mean, said, "You better save your money 'cause you'll be old." Here I'm 22 - "and you won't be able to play." I said, "I'll be playing when I'm 100 years old." And I believe so. That's from here, you know, because I'll be playing because he made a dirty remark. I'm about 22 and he's going to tell me I'm not going to play, save your money, and all that. But I like classical music and as I told you before I get my inspirations from it. But I don't want to go into it. I had 5 Juilliard pianists that come here for lessons and I had to let them all go because they taught them with their hands up here. Jazz you hug the keys. Like when the phone rang Hilton called me, Hilton Ruiz, I helped him, piano. He was doing all this with his hands up too high. I said, "You better drop your hands down on those keys." But probably with his fingers like that, he was fast.
(PHONE RINGS)
About kids playing.
WILLIAMS 183
Oh, about the position of the hands.

You see, that's something else. Now, I'm going to play classical music, I'm sure, before I die, because ever since a little kid I wanted to do that. But I'm so involved with this and these other things that I like about jazz, see. I'm going to write some classical things and play them. The greatest concert pianist, Robert Harris - I don't think you met him but he's usually at my parties - he teaches over at Juilliard and if you ever want to know the piano and learn how to play the piano, get to him. I hurt my fingers and I went to him and he gave me exercises to do, just not on the keys but other things to do. His teacher was the teacher of Clyde - what's his name - that went to Europe, the young kid that went to Europe -
Van Cliburn.
Van Cliburn, yes, and so he is sensational in teaching.
Is it really possible to shift over to classical music after -

Very possible. I had a pupil here and she was playing Bach and I had to teach her how to memorize and how to really play it. In about 5 minutes I was playing 4 bars. You understand? You know what classical music is - something that somebody's written and you do exercises on it in your woodshed and play it. But jazz is difficult. You think what
WILLIAMS 184

they've written and you have to play it then. So why should I want to play something somebody else has written? When I was a kid and my principal got all these teachers and all these things for me, I couldn't play Rachmaninoff and any of those things. I had to improvise in it. I couldn't play it the way the music was. I can't play music - when I'm reading, I have to improvise then. I hear it and see it, you know. I'm improvising then; I can't play it the way it's written. I never could play anything note for note so it wouldn't be good for me.
Playing classical music?
Yes.
This I think would be your problem, because classical music is based on the fact that you play it as written; you interpret it but you play it as written.
Right, right.
Whereas you don't play that way.
No, I don't play that way at all. But a lot of musicians can. Dizzy can; he can play note for note and things, but I can't. I have to improvise or add something.
At this point what is it that you want to do that you're not doing, aside from playing classical music?
I'm doing everything I want to do now except there are certain things I want to do, reach, go as high as I can now for the sake of others and not for Mary Lou (or to die, uh.)
WILLIAMS 185
Go as high as you can in what sense?

In the music field, I mean reach the pinnacle for public relations and get a lot of things going, because I cannot help the poor if I haven't got any strength in myself or any power to do so. I found that out. I can feed a lot of mouths if I got strength to go to somebody and ask for it. The world is still based on phony things and so what I'm trying to do is to do as many things like - such things as that street being named after me but I think I was cut down a little bit. It didn't leave Kansas City. (LAUGHTER) Isn't that something? The biggest thing that ever happened in the world of music and it was put up on a high level and everything and not one public relations man was there that could spread it all over the world. I've never heard of such a thing. If you were there and saw what went down - I don't think they knew what they were doing or they didn't exploit it right. That was a big deal. That was the biggest deal you ever heard of.
I think you should mention for the sake of the tape -
What?
For the sake of the tape that we should mention what you're retalking about.
The Charlie Parker Foundation and the streets that were named after such artists as Ella Fitzgerald, Count Basie,
WILLIAMS 186

Bennie Moten, Mary Lou Williams, and Dizzy Gillespie, five of us. But it was the way in which they did it. It was a big deal. I know they must have spent a fortune doing it, had a party and Gloria Vanderbilt, her husband, and the Hallmark people were sponsoring the Charlie Parker Foundation.
Were they the sponsors for it?

Yeah, they own practically Kansas City and this Hotel they built, it opened the same day that I got there. The governor, the mayor, and oh, just a big thing. Duke Ellington was there, Count Basie with his band, but no big exploitation on the outside of Kansas City. They raised a lot of money and they charged about $50 a plate. Had 2 or 3 nights of that.
That was a big deal and what's it called, Charlie Parker Houses?
Charlie Parker Foundation.
But it's a housing development, and these are the streets in the housing development and the housing development is named after Charlie Parker.
Right. /We were trying to get you to go there.
Oh, they were after me to go.

None of the newspaper men - Leonard Feather had to do something and the guy with the New Yorker and all the newspaper men should have been there. Look at the Newport Jazz Festival. They all went there at one time or another.
WILLIAMS
But none of them came from out of the -
From a distance. I want to get the argument about how these things break. How do you feel now? You've lived your life -
But I don't feel that I have. I don't know if I'm old, white, or black.
You haven't finished it. It's still going on, sure. But how do you feel about how it's worked out for you so far?
Beautiful. I'd live it again, go over the same things, one-nighters with Andy Kirk, starvation, and many, many things that happened. I'd go over it again.
If you went over it again do you feel that you would do it any better than you did it this time?

I think we all would if we experienced a lot of things. We'd know how to do them, but I think we'd do worse if we haven't experienced anything. But if I have experienced something and had to go over it again I think I'd do it better.
Most of us would. Well, any thing more you want to say?
Not right now. I'll remember something when you get home.
We'll pick it up later then.
O.K.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: Copyright notice and Smithsonian interview heading
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright warnings and the title page: Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Project, Mary Lou Williams interviewed by John S. Wilson on 6/26/1973.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: Birth in Atlanta, her father's name, and meeting him in 1952
segments.summary: Born in Atlanta in 1910 as Mary Louise Scruggs, out of wedlock. She finally met her father in 1952 through her half-brother Willis; his first words were asking what she had brought him.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: Family silence about the past; learning she was born out of wedlock
segments.summary: Her family never talked about backgrounds, so she listened under the bed. A relative's angry remark at 10 or 12 told her she was illegitimate; she shrugged it off and went out to play.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: Her mother Virginia Burley and the first melodies on her lap
segments.summary: Her mother played church piano and organ; Mary Lou picked out melodies at 2 or 3 and her mother called the neighbours. Professional pianists like Jack Howard were brought in to play around her.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: No teachers, perfect pitch, and why she thinks studying is risky for jazz
segments.summary: Her mother allowed no teachers; she later found she had perfect pitch. She argues that studying can destroy it and the feeling in a self-taught music like jazz, and says God steered her.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: Brothers and sisters
segments.summary: She had many brothers and sisters, including twins born on her own birthday in a different year.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: Repeated cover page and the start of the questions
segments.summary: The cover page and opening questions are repeated (page re-scan), ending with a note about East Liberty in Pittsburgh.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: Leaving Atlanta, her mother's family and who was musical
segments.summary: She left Atlanta at 3 or 4. Her mother's family, including a great-grandmother, all came from Atlanta; only she and her mother were musical, apart from a twin brother who danced.

segments.chapter: Atlanta birth and family
segments.title: The first tunes: Fandango and Mother Pin a Rose on Me
segments.summary: She did not know what she was playing as a baby; later she played a ragtime tune her mother taught her, 'Fandango', and a song her stepfather Fletcher Burley taught her.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Why the family moved to Pittsburgh and where they lived
segments.summary: The family followed relatives to Pittsburgh. Her mother married Fletcher Burley about a year later, and they moved through three or four homes in East Liberty.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: The little girl who played for money and with a union band
segments.summary: As a child she played for teas and neighbours, charging a dollar an hour. At 10 or 12 she played with a union band by ear without reading, and musicians took her out with her mother's trust.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: What she played: Fats Waller, the player piano and family allowances
segments.summary: She learned classics from a player piano, copied Fats Waller records, and was paid by her grandfather, uncle and stepfather to play their favourites; she still preferred jazz.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: The 'little piano girl of East Liberty' and the Pittsburgh parties
segments.summary: From 6 to 14 she played the parties of wealthy Pittsburgh families, including the Mellons, and her brother-in-law took her to theatres to listen.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Roland Mayfield, the Black Prince of East Liberty
segments.summary: Roland Mayfield was a nightclub owner who taught her to drive and always rescued her when she was stranded on the road.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Jack Howard's influence on her left hand
segments.summary: Jack Howard taught her to play the left hand louder than the right and many professional things; he followed her mother's circle from Atlanta to Pittsburgh.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Her stepfather Fletcher Burley, gambler and protector
segments.summary: Fletcher Burley loved her, was generous and feared in Pittsburgh, and took her into gambling joints under a big coat to play. Mayfield again rescued her from stranded tours.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: McKinney's Cotton Pickers take her out on gigs
segments.summary: When McKinney's Cotton Pickers, including Chu Berry, visited Pittsburgh they picked up the schoolgirl and took her on jobs.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Leaving professionally with Buzzin' Harris's TOBA vaudeville show
segments.summary: A touring show's pianist fell ill; she memorised the whole show from the owner's humming and played that night. She toured Ohio and Indiana for two months with comedian Brodson (Buzzin') Harris's weekly TOBA vaudeville.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Running away to play and dating the Seymour and Jeanette stockings
segments.summary: She ran away to be with musicians until her mother fetched her. She dates the first job with Seymour and Jeanette to about 1925-26 from stockings she still keeps.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Her mother retrieves her from the home talent show
segments.summary: On a home-talent show in Washington, Pennsylvania, her mother found out where she was and picked her up. She says her playing was already known to musicians as far as New York.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: The manager who gave the girls whiskey, and Margaret Warren
segments.summary: The show's manager gave three girls whiskey in Coca-Cola; the older dancer Margaret Warren came in and beat him with a stick. Margaret watched over her again on the Harris show.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Listening to Fats Waller, Jelly Roll Morton and Willie the Lion
segments.summary: In Pittsburgh she studied Fats Waller, Jelly Roll Morton and Willie the Lion records; Morton later corrected her version of 'Pearls' in New York.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: John Williams and his combo join the Harris show
segments.summary: John Williams, whom she later married, joined the Buzzin' Harris show in Cleveland with a combo, won her mother's confidence, and had a trombonist, Sylvester Briscoe, who played with his foot.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Her role with the Harris show and the clowning of the jazz-band era
segments.summary: She played for the show, danced when a chorus girl was short, and did comic piano tricks like playing with a sheet over the keys; the 1920s combos clowned a lot.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Brother-in-law's alto, practising, and protection from police
segments.summary: Her brother-in-law Hugh Floyd's alto drove her to hit him with a lamp. She practised all day, the police made her play concerts, and she says a strange protection kept her safe.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Joining John Williams's combo and how she felt about him
segments.summary: She joined John's six-piece combo in the Harris show to get away from home. She admired him as a person but did not love him enough to marry, and the group toured small towns in Indiana, Ohio and Oklahoma.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Carnivals and circuses with Doc Cheatham
segments.summary: The group played circuses and carnivals, which she hated, with Doc Cheatham, Briscoe and guitarist Joe Williams, scraping by on little money.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Seymour and Jeanette send for John Williams's combo for $75 a week
segments.summary: Seymour and Jeanette were the only black act on the Keith and Pantages circuits. They wired for John's combo at $75 each, a fortune compared to $25.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: The rehearsal where Seymour first discovers a woman pianist
segments.summary: At the first rehearsal Seymour tried to have the girl removed from the piano until she played; then they accepted her. Seymour died within a year and the group was stranded in New York.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: The Lincoln Theatre with Ellington's Washingtonians, and Fats Waller
segments.summary: Stranded in New York, she played the Lincoln Theatre in Harlem with Seymour and Jeanette alongside Duke Ellington's Washingtonians and met Fats Waller, who made audiences scream.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Fats Waller throws her in the air at Connie's Inn
segments.summary: At Connie's Inn a friend bet that she could play everything Fats Waller composed. She did and Waller threw her up in the air; she then talks of the woman pianist Lovey Austin.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: Lovey Austin writing music at the piano
segments.summary: As a child she watched Lovey Austin write music with a cigarette for the next act and decided to do the same, as she later did for Benny Goodman and Kirk.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh childhood and touring shows
segments.title: End of reel
segments.summary: The interviewer ends this reel.

segments.chapter: Visions, names and Jelly Roll
segments.title: Birth under a veil and seeing spirits as a toddler
segments.summary: She was born with a veil, in a place thought to have been a Civil War cemetery, and saw a white dog turn into a cow. Her mother thought she was seeing spirits.

segments.chapter: Visions, names and Jelly Roll
segments.title: Ghosts in hotels on the Andy Kirk tours
segments.summary: On tour with Andy Kirk she would see apparitions in bad hotels and her husband had to tie her in bed.

segments.chapter: Visions, names and Jelly Roll
segments.title: ESP and how it fed into her music
segments.summary: She says ESP should go into the music: she could hear the next note a musician would play. It cannot be controlled.

segments.chapter: Visions, names and Jelly Roll
segments.title: Seeing people who were not there
segments.summary: She tells of warning her brother-in-law about a man in the street and grabbing the wheel on tour for an old couple who were not there.

segments.chapter: Visions, names and Jelly Roll
segments.title: Her mother's first husband Mose Winn and the names Winn and Burley
segments.summary: Her mother's first husband was Mose Winn; Mary Lou used Winn and Burley interchangeably as a girl.

segments.chapter: Visions, names and Jelly Roll
segments.title: How Jack Kapp changed her name to Mary Lou Williams
segments.summary: Before Jack Kapp at Decca named her Mary Lou Williams after her marriage, she had always been Burley, after her stepfather.

segments.chapter: Visions, names and Jelly Roll
segments.title: Visiting Jelly Roll Morton in New York
segments.summary: Before the Harris show, someone took her to Morton's office, where he roughly corrected her playing of 'Pearls'. She was not writing then.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Memphis: marrying John, forming a union and the Lunceford friendship
segments.summary: After Seymour died the group ended up in Memphis, where she married John Williams. He organised the musicians into a union, raising pay from $2 a night, and was a friend and checkers rival of Jimmy Lunceford.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Menace in Memphis: lynching threats, the streetcar and the kidnap plot
segments.summary: At a club outside Memphis she was threatened as a Northerner. She worked for Mrs. Singleton, was frightened on a streetcar, and had to leave when a Mississippi farmer paid the cook to kidnap her.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: John joins the band; Jimmy Lunceford fills in for him in Memphis
segments.summary: The Williams combo was doing well at the White Rose when John left to join a band; Lunceford replaced him for six months while she finished dates. She also relates the band's meeting about T. Holder.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Driving to Oklahoma City
segments.summary: She drove John's old Chevrolet 600 miles from Memphis to Oklahoma City with his mother, fixing tyres herself thanks to Roland Mayfield's training.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Arriving in Oklahoma City: sitting in with the band and its gentlemen
segments.summary: At first she was only John's wife, driving and called in to play 'Froggy Bottom' when the band was stuck. She remembers the musicians as young, well-dressed gentlemen.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: How the Kirk band rehearsed and its range of styles
segments.summary: The band made arrangements on the spot, played for white and black dances, could sound like Guy Lombardo or Basie, and its musicians inspired her to start arranging.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Andy Kirk takes over from T. Holder
segments.summary: Within three months the band voted out T. Holder, who had gambled the pay, and made Andy Kirk leader. She travelled with them but did not join as a member until 1931.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: The band's territory and how Kansas City became its base
segments.summary: The band toured Oklahoma, Arkansas and the Midwest, with Tulsa in summer. Kansas City became its base after the Playmore job, about two years after John joined.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: She starts to write arrangements
segments.summary: She gave ideas at rehearsals that Andy took down, then wrote her first full arrangement for him. She describes finding unusual chords that he said broke the rules.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Being called in at the Savoy against Chick Webb, but not hired
segments.summary: At the Savoy in New York the band called her in to break up Chick Webb's cutting contest, yet she was not made a regular member, partly because of the pianist Jack and because a woman was unusual.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: The Pearl Theatre in Philadelphia and the double piano
segments.summary: Billed as Blanche Calloway at the Pearl Theatre, Andy put her on a small piano beside Jack on a Steinway. When Jack fell ill she took the big piano and was kept.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Recording with Blanche Calloway and the Brunswick date
segments.summary: She sorts out the order of events: Blanche Calloway's Victor session came first, then the Pearl Theatre, then Brunswick refused to record Kirk unless she was there.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Her first solo record for Jack Kapp
segments.summary: She went to Chicago where Kapp recorded her playing what she thought was an audition. 'Night Life' became her first record, for which she was never paid.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Sorting out the chronology: Chicago, the Pearl and joining the band
segments.summary: She and the interviewer untangle the order: Chicago recording was the band's start, the Pearl came before, and the Pearl is where she became a regular member.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Wehnwood Beach and the first Decca sessions
segments.summary: After the Pearl the band played Wehnwood Beach and Fairyland, then recorded for Decca in New York every day for weeks; she wrote about twenty tunes in a week.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: The tunes she wrote for Decca, including Messa Stomp
segments.summary: She lists the pieces: 'Froggy Bottom', 'Messa Stomp', 'A Lot of Sax Appeal', 'Mary's Idea' and 'Cloudy'. She did most arranging with Andy until Earl Thompson came in.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Piney Brown's place, Joe Turner and Martha Raye in Kansas City
segments.summary: After their nightly work the band went to Piney Brown's, where Joe Turner, Pete Johnson and Hot Lips Page played, and Martha Raye, on her way to Hollywood, stayed to sing.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Martha Raye, Sleepy and Lincoln: pianists of Kansas City
segments.summary: Martha Raye stayed two weeks. She recalls Sleepy, who played like Art Tatum in the hard keys, and Lincoln, the only pianist Martha would sing with.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Lester Young replaces Ben Webster; the era of well-trained musicians
segments.summary: Lester Young joined Kirk after Webster left for Cab Calloway, before going to Basie. She compares Lester's freedom with Webster's economy, and says the era bred Parker and Dizzy.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Women pianists in Kansas City
segments.summary: She says other women played like men, among them Julia Lee, but she was unique in an all-male band, and afterwards some bands in St. Louis hired girls.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: Charlie Parker in Kansas City and the Moten versus Basie beat
segments.summary: At Wehnwood Beach she heard Parker playing with Andy Kirk's wife, and the boys did not understand him. Kansas City wanted a steady swing; Basie lightened Moten's beat.

segments.chapter: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
segments.title: End of tape and an out-of-sequence note
segments.summary: The tape ends, with a note that the following passage belongs later in the sequence.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Deering's Farm, the jam with Ellington's band, and Orlando Wright
segments.summary: Leading her own band at Deering's Farm, with singer Joe Williams, she hosted Duke Ellington's men. Orlando Wright astonished Ben Webster by playing 'Body and Soul' in all keys, and Art Blakey learned time.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Hal Baker goes to Ellington and her band falls apart
segments.summary: Her husband Harold Baker left overnight with Ellington. She tried Pittsburgh replacements and Kelly's Stable in New York but disbanded, while Fletcher Henderson hired Blakey's Pittsburghers.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Dewey Square Hotel, John Hammond and Cafe Society
segments.summary: Stranded, she stayed in the Dewey Square Hotel to think. Through John Hammond and Louise Crane, she was booked into Cafe Society downtown, where she stayed off and on for five years.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Cafe Society: Josh White, Barney Josephson and Johnny Garrett
segments.summary: At Cafe Society she worked solo. Johnny Garrett, the valet, made her smile with a Bronx cheer; Josh White and Imogene Coca are among those she remembers.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Recording for Moe Asch and Victor, and writing in her head
segments.summary: She recorded much for Moe Asch and for Victor ('Waltz Boogie'). She composed arrangements on the subway for her trio with J. C. Heard.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Hanging out on 52nd Street and jamming at her apartment
segments.summary: Around 1946-47 she followed the new musicians on 52nd Street, and Tadd Dameron, Bud Powell, Miles Davis and others jammed at her apartment.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Monk falls asleep in her apartment
segments.summary: Monk once entered her apartment and lay down in the other bed; her scream sent him into the closet. She says Monk replayed new tunes for months to see if they stuck.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Why she left Cafe Society
segments.summary: Cafe Society petered out after years and Glaser booked her away from the city; she wrote the 'Zodiac Suite' there and Josephson gave a Town Hall concert.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Norman Granz, Milton Orent and the Philharmonic offer
segments.summary: Norman Granz asked her to play with Jazz at the Philharmonic and got permission for the symphony. Milton Orent, a weird-sounding composer, taught her; they co-wrote 'In the Land of Oo-Bla-Dee' and she helped Miles with the tuba idea.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Writing the Zodiac Suite and the WNEW radio show
segments.summary: She began the suite for a WNEW radio programme, one sign a week, and when inspiration ran dry she improvised the rest and recorded it with Nola Studios.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: The Zodiac Suite at Carnegie Hall in 1946
segments.summary: With Orent called away, she finished the arrangements herself, writing a bop blues for 36 violins overnight with David Stone Martin, and slipped it past the manager. The musicians cheered.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Lost recordings and the Rome performance of the suite
segments.summary: Recordings of the Carnegie concert and the Town Hall concert were stolen. She later did the suite in Rome with an 18-piece group.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: The fights at Cafe Society
segments.summary: Wartime audiences from the South sometimes started fights; once a man grabbed her until Canada Lee cooled things down, and Doc Cheatham skated over the bar.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Working with Josh White and Barney Josephson's star-making idea
segments.summary: Josh White was a beautiful person to work with; Josephson booked unknown singers beside stars. She did many benefits at the Cafe.

segments.chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
segments.title: Moe Asch's love of artists, and bringing Erroll Garner and Art Tatum to him
segments.summary: Asch let artists record whatever they wanted. She brought in Erroll Garner and Art Tatum, who recorded for little money, and she took Asch's recordings to Pittsburgh.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Moe Gale sends her to England to break the union ban
segments.summary: After Glaser's bookings, Moe Gale sent her to England to break a thirty-year union ban; she played with Ted Heath and others and was held over eleven months.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Disliking life abroad; English food and the S.S. United cooks
segments.summary: She prefers America. Rationing was bad, so the S.S. United's crew brought her steaks; she slipped away rather than face a birthday party.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Playing Paris concert halls and Boeuf sur le Toit
segments.summary: In Paris she made more money than ever, playing concert halls and the Boeuf sur le Toit as a solo act.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: The Lascelles party and the 91st Psalm
segments.summary: At a party given by the Queen's cousin, a black GI told her to read the 91st Psalm; she read all of them and began to pray.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Garland Wilson's club in Paris and Gerard Pochonet
segments.summary: In Paris she worked Garland Wilson's club, then walked out unpaid; drummer Gerard Pochonet got her money and took her to the country. The tape ends.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Meeting Thelonious Monk in Kansas City in 1930
segments.summary: She met Monk, travelling with a medicine show, at a Kansas City club called the Subway. Nobody understood his playing, yet Lester Young and Basie went to hear him.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Originality in Kansas City and the Cherry Blossom jam sessions
segments.summary: Kansas City musicians all had individual styles. The Cherry Blossom was a place for after-show jamming.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Country and Judge Gershon
segments.summary: Country, chauffeur to Judge Gershon, helped musicians in trouble. She tells the story of Gershon hunting for him and his pawned Cadillac tyres.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Musicians and the law in Kansas City: race mixing under Prohibition
segments.summary: Black and white mixed drinking got boys picked up by a detective, but Country had them released. Segregation of streetcars disappeared in a year or so.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: White musicians and pupils in Kansas City
segments.summary: White musicians visited the black district, and she and Basie taught about thirty pupils, mostly white. Visiting whites played the Muehlebach Hotel.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Lucille, Louise and Rosita on Fifth Avenue
segments.summary: She tells of Stumpy Buddy and of two young women, Lucille and Louise, who followed musicians; their wildness at clubs, and Sammy Price expecting the piano to vanish.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Gangsters in Kansas City
segments.summary: Kansas City gangsters made Basie work without pay; a Kirk singer nearly got killed; the Luscoe brothers had the band afraid to fetch their beer.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Nothing rubbed off on her in Kansas City
segments.summary: She says music was all that mattered, staying up days and nights playing.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Florence Mills, Ziegfeld and the Harlem theatre scene
segments.summary: At 14 to 16 she met Florence Mills through Jeanette. She relates Ziegfeld's way of handling singers, and describes Mills as sweet and delicate, like Josephine Baker.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Moms Mabley, John Mason and Bojangles at the Tree of Hope
segments.summary: She met comedians Moms Mabley and John Mason, and Bill Bojangles, who could run backwards as fast as others ran forwards.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: Florence Mills remembered
segments.summary: Mills was a dancer and singer, in the Ziegfeld show 'Poor Little Blackbird'; she was sad when Mills died.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: The Rhythm Club jam session with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: John Williams took her to the Rhythm Club, where Armstrong, Benny Carter, Hodges and Fats Waller jammed; he made her play. Armstrong was like a god among them.

segments.chapter: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
segments.title: A week at Connie's Inn after Waller
segments.summary: At Connie's Inn her swinging feet fascinated the dancers; she earned $75 a week, which helped the stranded group.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Monk at Minton's in the 1930s
segments.summary: She saw Monk in New York in the 1930s and grew close at Minton's, where bop musicians jammed because 52nd Street had no work for them.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Monk's rehearsal big band and the real beginning of bebop
segments.summary: Monk and Bud Powell rehearsed in a basement to create a new music for recognition; she says Dizzy created real bebop and Monk worked for Dizzy.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Subbing for Dizzy at a dance: $6, a strike and the union board
segments.summary: Leading Dizzy's group at a ballroom, she refused to play at intermission until pay was raised; the union board nearly fined them but made her a member.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Bud Powell, Monk's big band and the house that built bop
segments.summary: Bud idolised Monk and played his compositions; the big band disbanded and everyone jammed at Minton's, 'the house that built bop'.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Being thrown out of clubs and jamming in New York
segments.summary: Before Minton's, she and Dick Wilson, Lester Young and others opened clubs that threw them out once business was good; one jam spot beat a union delegate.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Downtown musicians at Minton's, and older musicians' resentment
segments.summary: Downtown players copied phrases on cuffs; older musicians resented bop, and she lost friends among them.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Her apartment with the white carpet
segments.summary: Monk, Bud, Dameron, Dizzy, Miles, Sarah Vaughan and others came to her apartment to write and play; she has had the carpet since 1941.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Dissatisfied with older music, fired from Cafe Society
segments.summary: She was fired for lateness and glad, because the new music on 52nd Street gave her a new picture; Barney hired her back.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: Helping arrangers and getting inspiration from modern classical records
segments.summary: She helped Tadd Dameron out of arranging jams and draws inspiration from Schoenberg and Delius records.

segments.chapter: Minton's, bop and the Monk circle
segments.title: How ideas come, dry spells and why she won't be a hired arranger
segments.summary: Ideas come from nowhere or from the subway wheels; she runs dry and will not take a job as arranger. She creates best playing with a bass player.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
segments.title: Miss Milholland, the principal who helped a gifted black child
segments.summary: In grade school Miss Milholland let her arrive late, booked her gigs at Tech University and took her home to play.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
segments.title: Slavery stories, hitting her teacher, and the Pittsburgh school
segments.summary: Overhearing her great-grandparents' slavery tales so angered her that she hit teacher Miss Itzel. She argues children should hear the whole history of black America.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
segments.title: Roland Mayfield teaches her to drive, race and fix cars
segments.summary: Mayfield taught the girls to drive and race on Bigelow Boulevard; she fixed a car on a trip and Mayfield broke up gangs at Earl Hines's dances.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
segments.title: Bands in Pittsburgh, the Subway club and Buck and Bubbles
segments.summary: Visiting bands took her on gigs, and Roland gave her a car. At the Subway on Wiley Avenue she met Buck of Buck and Bubbles, a pianist equal to Waller.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
segments.title: Buck's secret run and Art Tatum
segments.summary: Buck taught her a run, in reverse, so that Tatum and Basie played it wrong for years.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
segments.title: Jealousy: the razor, the husband's girls and the wives who watched her
segments.summary: Jealousy was mostly about women: a trumpeter's wife pulled a razor on her; a Tulsa woman wanted her dead; the Kirk wives quietly protected her.

segments.chapter: Pittsburgh school days and old jealousies
segments.title: Ben Webster, her first love
segments.summary: Ben Webster came from a wealthy family and was too wild to marry; he calmed down after a year in the Kirk band.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Mildred Bailey at the 18th Hole and Stella Brooks's heckling
segments.summary: She worked with Mildred Bailey and George Auld's band; Stella Brooks, a singer, upset the singers, including Bailey, by making faces.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Mildred Bailey's personality
segments.summary: Bailey was jolly with her; she had split from Red Norvo and once got sick on Andy Kirk's barbecue.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Working 52nd Street with Billy Taylor and the barred Birdland musicians
segments.summary: At a club alternating with Billy Taylor she hired Oscar Pettiford, Kenny Clarke, Kai Winding and others who were barred from Birdland; Milt Jackson's playing showed her how to accompany.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Oscar Pettiford, composing and the Moscow Mule
segments.summary: With Pettiford she composed several tunes a night; his drinking led her to move him to cello and hire Percy Heath.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Charlie Parker plays the Kansas City Blues
segments.summary: Parker asked to get a band together; she had him play, and he played a blues for the packed crowd with changes she had never heard.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: The Woody Herman band, walking out, and the offer to go to Europe
segments.summary: Glaser replaced her sidemen without warning with a Woody Herman group. She walked out, then Gale's office called with the English ban offer.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Looking after Bud Powell
segments.summary: Bud Powell was sensitive and unstable; she took him home when he went off, called him by Monk's name to calm him, and he never stole.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Charlie Parker as a friend, and hearing his strings
segments.summary: Parker consulted her on his writing, asked her to hear the strings at Birdland, and returned her stolen pocketbook.

segments.chapter: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
segments.title: Miles Davis, the tuba and his troubles
segments.summary: She credits a casual chat about tubas for Miles's nine-piece sound; she describes Miles in Birdland and what she heard of his later problems.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Max Roach's politics
segments.summary: She disagrees with Max Roach's political approach to racial mistreatment; she says it distracts from her music.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Her own politics and why she never voted
segments.summary: She was drawn into politics through benefits but concluded to stick to music; a clarinet player's voting story put her off voting.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Africa and why she would not go
segments.summary: She knew Africa's history from her great-grandparents, says she could not live there and argues black Americans should fight for freedom at home.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Muslims and other religions the musicians turned to
segments.summary: She went through many religions in the late 1940s as musicians became Muslims. Everything introduced in America becomes an evil, she says.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: The Jehovah's Witnesses and her own fanaticism
segments.summary: She disliked their pamphlets and says dealing with God can make one a fanatic; Father Woods offered her a psychiatrist.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: How she got into it: the party in England and the 91st Psalm again
segments.summary: She retells the English party where a GI recommended the 91st Psalm, the S.S. United steaks, and leaving for Paris.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: What reading the Psalms did to her
segments.summary: She says the Psalms uprooted her and freed her from being stuck, a magic that you have to experience.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Garland Wilson's illness and working the Boeuf sur le Toit
segments.summary: Garland Wilson died soon after arriving; she took over his job, doubled at a theatre, then walked off both jobs.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Tape change
segments.summary: The interviewer stops while tapes are changed.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Staying with Gerard Pochonet's grandmother and praying
segments.summary: Pochonet took her to the country, where she stayed six to eight months, cancelled work and only prayed, eating and sleeping.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Psychic visions: predictions for jazz and Charlie Parker's death
segments.summary: While praying she foresaw Parker's death and a strange sound that would harm jazz, tracing jazz from spirituals to bop.

segments.chapter: Politics, Africa, religion and the Paris conversion
segments.title: Returning home: Charlie Parker, the riots and Father Woods
segments.summary: She wanted to come home to help musicians, as Parker was in trouble. She says Father Woods got her back to music.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Father Woods and Barry Ulanov
segments.summary: Father Woods was her confessor, arranged for her by Barry Ulanov; she began going to church once back in America.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Baptist childhood and the insurance man's Bible
segments.summary: She came out of the Baptist church as a girl; an admirer in Kirk days gave her a Bible she never read until after Europe.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Trying other churches, and choosing the Catholic church
segments.summary: She tried several churches, including a dancer-turned-preacher in Harlem, before settling on the Catholic church where she could meditate.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Father Crowley and friends feeding her
segments.summary: Father Crowley called her a saint; she housed and fed people and Dizzy and Lorraine Gillespie sent food.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: How Father Woods came to instruct her
segments.summary: Father Crowley told Ulanov, who found Woods, a Jesuit beloved by musicians; he helped her back to music.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Why she stopped playing
segments.summary: She says praying took her away from playing and she chose to help people in the flesh.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Priests, Dizzy and Melba get her to Newport
segments.summary: Priests, Dizzy and Melba Liston coaxed her out to the Newport Jazz Festival, while she was fasting.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: The Composer Room and the Hickory House comeback
segments.summary: Her return to clubs was terrible: at the Composer Room she hid in the checkroom, and Father Woods sat with her at the Hickory House.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Writing music for St. Martin de Porres
segments.summary: After St. Martin's canonization in 1962 she wrote a piece and Father Woods wrote the lyric.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Babs Gonzales and the stolen book of slang
segments.summary: Babs Gonzales had his slang book published by a disc jockey and became bitter; she tried to calm him.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Taking Monk and Bud to church
segments.summary: Monk, Hal Baker and Bud Powell met her at Our Lady of Lourdes; Monk drank wine first and fell in the door.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Bel Canto Foundation: helping musicians off heroin with prayers and music
segments.summary: She helped addict musicians by keeping them with her and having them play drum parts she wrote.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: What the Bel Canto Foundation was
segments.summary: A foundation to help addicts and alcoholics; her lawyer thought the board strange.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: The Bel Canto thrift store
segments.summary: She sold donated clothes in a Harlem store, which she gave up when the Hickory House job began.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Father Peter O'Brien
segments.summary: A young Jesuit she met at the Hickory House called from California and returned to help her.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: The Wells Restaurant venture
segments.summary: She played at Wells in Harlem and lost $12,000 after a disagreement; she quit the day Kennedy was shot.

segments.chapter: Church, Bel Canto and the return to music
segments.title: Returning to Cafe Society with Peter O'Brien
segments.summary: Barney Josephson put in a piano; the union scale cost her thousands; young people came after the rock clubs closed.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: The lean years: royalties and friends
segments.summary: She had few jobs and survived on royalties and friends like Dizzy and Lorraine.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Philharmonic Hall with Dizzy's band
segments.summary: With Father Woods's help, she and Dizzy were first jazz unit in the Philharmonic, doing a history of jazz.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: How Alvin Ailey came to her Mass
segments.summary: Peter and Brother John Sellers pushed her and Ailey toward the ballet.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Ailey's ballet and 'People in Trouble'
segments.summary: Ailey adapted her Mass; she explains the song 'People in Trouble' was for the Harlem rioters.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: What the ballet did for her career
segments.summary: It gave recognition among new audiences but no club work.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: She is a jazz pianist before a composer
segments.summary: She says piano comes first; arranging came from Kansas City and she lost records she had not copyrighted.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Copyright and composing while playing
segments.summary: She starts a melody to copyright, and composes best at the piano.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: End of tape
segments.summary: The interviewer ends the tape.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Praying for souls and the candle dream
segments.summary: She prayed for priests and souls and dreamed about lighting candles, and her aunt appeared in chains.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Levy's death, brown candles and visits in dreams
segments.summary: Birdland's Levy came for a prayer and was killed; she burned brown candles and had dreams of the dead.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: ESP returning to her music
segments.summary: The ESP moved back into her music as she played more; she sees less now.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: The beaded pocketbook and Lorraine Gillespie
segments.summary: She overheard Lorraine and Dizzy discussing a pocketbook she could not sell, and returned it to Hazel Scott.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Cardinal Wright and the Pittsburgh jazz festival
segments.summary: Bishop Wright arranged festivals in Pittsburgh with Father Woods's help; she left them to George Wein.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Copenhagen and the jazz Mass in Rome, 1968
segments.summary: She opened a club in Copenhagen and tried a jazz Mass in Rome, which the Vatican radio spoiled.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Going to church now
segments.summary: She now goes on Sundays; daily mass gave her strength against the world.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: A woman in a man's world
segments.summary: Being among men taught her their thinking; Monk said she was the only woman he'd listen to.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Women musicians and acceptance
segments.summary: She withdraws from contests with women, was always accepted by men, and recalls Earl Hines in Pittsburgh.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Classical music, rock and jazz
segments.summary: She learned classics from the player piano and won't play rock because it stiffens her feel.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Classical ambitions, Juilliard pianists and Robert Harris
segments.summary: She plans classical writing, dismissed Juilliard pianists with high hands, and credits Robert Harris.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Why she cannot play note for note
segments.summary: She always improvises, even reading Rachmaninoff.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: What she still wants to do
segments.summary: She wants to rise in music for the sake of the poor; the street naming in Kansas City was badly promoted.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: The Charlie Parker Foundation streets in Kansas City
segments.summary: Five streets in a housing development named after Parker foundation, including hers, with sponsorship by Hallmark.

segments.chapter: Later career and reflections
segments.title: Looking back and goodbyes
segments.summary: She would live it again, one-nighters and starvation included, and the interview closes.
